Title: Exploring the Nexus of technology, environmental policy stringency, and political globalization: Pathways to achieving sustainability
Authors: Mubeen Abdur Rehman, Mudassar Hasan, Ugur Korkut Pata, Xihui Haviour Chen, Andreas Kontoleon
Abstract: This study examines the effects of technology patents, environmental policy stringency, and political globalization on green energy markets and energy transitions in 18 OECD countries from 1990 to 2022. Two models—one focusing on renewable energy and the other on non-renewable energy—were analyzed using Method of Moments Quantile Regression (MMQR), which accounts for outliers and nonlinear relationships. The results demonstrate that technological advancement and stringent environmental policies promote the adoption of renewable energy. Additionally, political globalization shows a positive correlation with green energy while negatively impacting fossil fuel use. The study offers policy recommendations for advancing green energy transitions aligned with the net-zero carbon agenda.

Title: Trading electrons: Predicting DART spread spikes in ISO electricity markets
Authors: Emma Hubert, Dimitrios Lolas, Ronnie Sircar
Abstract: We study the problem of forecasting and optimally trading day-ahead versus real-time (DART) price spreads in U.S. wholesale electricity markets. Building on the framework of Galarneau-Vincent et al., we extend spike prediction from a single zone to a multi-zone setting and treat both positive and negative DART spikes within a unified statistical model. To translate directional signals into economically meaningful positions, we develop a structural and market-consistent price impact model based on day-ahead bid stacks. This yields closed-form expressions for the optimal vector of zonal INC/DEC quantities, capturing asymmetric buy/sell impacts and cross-zone congestion effects. When applied to NYISO, the resulting impact-aware strategy significantly improves the risk-return profile relative to unit-size trading and highlights substantial heterogeneity across markets and seasons.

Title: Financing the low-carbon transition: Do energy transition investments improve ESG performance?
Authors: Kwamie Dunbar, Mohammed Alrashdani
Abstract: Energy transition investment ( eti ) has emerged as a central component of global climate finance, yet its firm-level consequences remain insufficiently understood. Using BloombergNEF energy-transition investment data and Refinitiv ESG measures, we examine whether aggregate transition-finance deployment influences corporate sustainability performance. We find that higher eti exposure is associated with significant improvements in environmental, social, and governance ( esg ) performance, with the strongest gains observed in the environmental pillar. The positive association is stronger among firms with greater climate-related innovative capacity and among low-carbon firms, whereas esg gains are comparatively smaller in high-carbon sectors despite the economic importance of eti for managing transition risk. Robustness analyses based on dynamic System Generalized Method of Moments (SGMM) estimation, external instrumental-variable techniques, and Granger-causality tests indicate that eti precedes and predicts subsequent esg improvements. Overall, the findings identify a macro-to-micro transmission mechanism through which large-scale transition-finance deployment shapes firm behavior and sustainability outcomes, establishing eti as an important driver of multidimensional corporate sustainability performance.

Title: Regional collaborative emission reduction under carbon transfer: A differential game analysis of China's three major urban agglomerations
Authors: Ze Yang, Haoning Li, Yuchen Zhang, Yongling Li

Title: Climate risk perception, performance feedback and corporate environmental responsibility

Title: Presidents, prices at the pump, and the difference in perceptions between energy market experts and non-experts
Authors: Dylan Brewer, Matthew E. Oliver
Abstract: We conduct a survey of US-based energy market experts and non-experts and find that non-experts are significantly more likely to believe the US President plays a major role in determining retail fuel prices. Next, we analyze weekly retail gasoline and diesel price data from the US, UK, France, and Canada under different heads of state. After controlling for fluctuations in the wholesale crude oil price, country-specific long-run averages in prices, common time shocks, and national fuel excise taxes, we find that fuel prices differ systematically across leaders, though not universally. Although we do not claim to have established a causal link between executive regime change and retail fuel price variation, our fuel price analysis does help explain why many people believe political executives can influence retail gasoline prices, a phenomenon with important political and macroeconomic ramifications.

Title: Designing renewable energy auctions for high realization probability — CfD and payment-only auctions
Authors: Runxi Wang, Karl-Martin Ehrhart
Abstract: In recent years, different instruments for renewable energy expansion have been debated. Among the support and hedging instruments, two-sided contracts for difference (CfDs) have become the default in many countries and are promoted by the European Commission. On the other hand, payment-only auctions have also become established, where the electricity sales are unregulated, but the winners must pay for the right to build energy plants. Focusing on a high realization probability and the induced welfare effects, we compare two-sided CfDs with payment-only auctions. Contrary to the conventional wisdom, the non-realization risk is higher with auctioned CfDs than with payment-only auctions and is exacerbated by risk aversion, when developers can cope with both options. CfDs are particularly useful when developers need support for implementing their projects. Against this backdrop and considering asymmetric information, i.e., developers know best the economic conditions of their projects, we propose a design in which developers decide competitively between a CfD auction and a payment-only auction and which enhances the realization probability.

Title: Macroeconomic risk, political instability, and environmental sustainability risk: assessing vulnerabilities among emerging and developing economies
Authors: Rexford Abaidoo, Ayodele Julius Alade, Elvis Kwame Agyapong
Abstract: This empirical inquiry examines the impact of environmental sustainability risk (ESR) on political agitations and macroeconomic risk among emerging and developing economies in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). ESR is examined from three main perspectives: the extent of carbon emissions (denoted by CO 2 emissions), coverage or the extent of exploitation of land and water resources (denoted by the ecological footprint index), and unsustainable exploitation of natural resources (denoted by genuine sustainability risk). Data for the analysis were compiled for a sample of 36 countries from the sub-region, and empirical estimates were conducted using pooled ordinary least squares with Driscoll and Kraay standard errors, as well as the two-step system GMM framework. Empirical findings from the study show that growth in CO 2 emissions heightens macroeconomic risk among the examined economies. The results further suggest that an increase in ecological footprint exacerbates political instability for the examined economies in the sub-region. Additionally, the reported results indicate that effective governance and institutional structures can help mitigate the adverse impact of environmental sustainability risks on macroeconomic risks and political instability in the reviewed developing and emerging economies.

Title: Fuel taxes without borders: Tax-induced price changes and recorded fuel sales in the European Union
Authors: Janez Dolšak
Abstract: This paper estimates how retail fuel prices and cross-border price differentials affect recorded domestic road-fuel sales in the European Union, using harmonized monthly panel data for 24 countries from January 2008 through December 2025. We use tax-induced variation in retail prices, instrumenting domestic prices and relative price gaps with statutory fuel-tax variables in two-stage least squares models with country and month fixed effects. We complement the country-month analysis with directed dyadic IV specifications that compare home and neighbouring countries within land-border pairs. The outcome is recorded domestic fuel sales, not physical fuel consumption within national borders, so the estimates capture both changes in fuel use and shifts in the location where purchases are recorded. For diesel, the preferred country-month IV estimate implies an own-price elasticity of approximately −1.40 for recorded domestic road-diesel sales. For gasoline, the preferred estimate is also negative, approximately −0.78, although it is less stable across demanding sensitivity specifications. The clearest evidence of cross-border reallocation comes from the dyadic IV design. When the dyadic price differential is defined as the neighbour's log price minus the home country's log price, the cross-border coefficient is positive and close to +0.53 for both diesel and gasoline. This means that recorded domestic sales increase when neighbouring countries become more expensive relative to the home country. The findings imply that uncoordinated national fuel-tax changes can shift where purchases are recorded, potentially eroding domestic tax bases and complicating the interpretation of national fuel-sales statistics in integrated markets.

Title: Comparative research and analysis on third-party governance based on market effects
Authors: Zuliang Lu, Junman Li, Mingsong Li, Zhihui Cao, Zhuran Xiang
Abstract: With the tightening of environmental regulations, traditional command-and-control pollution approaches have proven inadequate. Specifically, they fail to align with the incentives of polluting enterprises, relying on coercion rather than motivation, and suffer from low treatment efficiency due to insufficient technical expertise. Specifically, they fail to align with the incentives of polluting enterprises, relying on coercion rather than motivation, and suffer from low treatment efficiency due to insufficient technical expertise. While prior research highlights its potential to enhance environmental governance, empirical validation remains limited. This study applies evolutionary game theory to compare two models, investigating the efficacy of third-party institutions in regional pollution control and the impact of key system parameters. Notably, we integrate external market and consumer factors as dynamic parameters. Our findings demonstrate that third-party participation yields significantly better evolutionary outcomes. Furthermore, stakeholder strategies exhibit strong interdependence, sensitive to parameter variations. Based on this comparative analysis, we offer evidence-based policy implications for optimizing third-party governance mechanisms.

Title: Dual channel mixed frequency forecasting for carbon prices: Informer-BiLSTM deep features embedded in Grey-MIDAS framework
Authors: Qi Ding, Xinping Xiao, Lizhong Yang, Zhuang Yang, Zhiwei Xu
Abstract: As global climate governance accelerates and carbon markets become increasingly financialized, carbon prices link macro level mitigation targets with micro level firm decision making. However, mixed frequency explanatory variables and recurrent structural breaks constrain forecasting performance, leaving econometric models with limited robustness. Using carbon prices in the EU Emissions Trading System and the China Emissions Trading System and incorporating 14 explanatory variables, this study develops a dual channel, feature driven mixed frequency grey forecasting model (GMIB) that combines the Informer model and bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM) to handle variable heterogeneity and frequency alignment. Trend dominated variables enter the Informer model to extract global features, whereas fluctuation dominated variables enter the BiLSTM model to capture high frequency shocks; both feature sets are integrated into a grey system based mixed data sampling (MIDAS) framework (Grey-MIDAS) to strengthen mixed frequency modeling capability. GMIB is evaluated against machine learning baselines, single frequency deep learning baselines, and mixed frequency deep learning baselines, and residual bootstrap intervals are constructed to quantify uncertainty and tail risk. Empirical evidence shows that GMIB delivers the most accurate point forecasts in both markets, achieving mean absolute percentage errors (MAPE) of 1.10% and 1.05%. Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) indicate that the China market is anchored by energy cost trends, whereas the EU market is more sensitive to financial sentiment shocks. Overall, the framework improves carbon price discovery, supports regulatory monitoring, corporate compliance, and financial institutions' risk management, and promotes the sustainable operation of carbon trading markets.

Title: Pumped hydro energy storage: Structural results and solution algorithms
Authors: Harun Avci, Ece Cigdem Karakoyun, Ayse Selin Kocaman, Emre Nadar, Parinaz Toufani
Abstract: We study a pumped hydro energy storage facility that consists of two interconnected reservoirs – an upper and a lower – where one reservoir may be fed by natural inflow. The system operator makes real-time decisions regarding the amount of water to pump or release, thereby determining the amount of electricity to buy from or sell to the market. We model this problem as a Markov decision process, accounting for uncertainties in both streamflow rates and electricity prices. We prove the optimality of a state-dependent threshold policy under positive electricity prices: The state space can be partitioned into several disjoint domains, each associated with a different action type, such that it is optimal to bring the total amount of water in the facility and the amount of water in the upper reservoir to a different pair of state-dependent target levels in each domain. For more general data-calibrated instances in which prices can be negative, we use this threshold structure as the basis for policy-approximation algorithms. These algorithms yield near-optimal solutions up to 28 times faster than brute-force optimization, with no significant drain on total cash flows compared to the optimal solution.

Title: Just transition? Exploring the climate finance, regulatory quality, trade openness and renewable energy nexus
Authors: Lili Wang, Jun Pang
Abstract: Climate finance aims to support a fair transition to renewable energy in developing countries, yet the conditions under which climate finance is associated with renewable energy development remain unclear. This study examines the relationship between climate finance and renewable energy development using a double machine learning (DML) framework that combines Lasso regression as the base learner with K-fold cross-fitting and Neyman orthogonalization to mitigate potential bias arising from endogeneity and high-dimensional confounding. Drawing on panel data from 71 developing countries over 2000–2019, the DML estimation yields a statistically significant positive association, and the positive association between climate finance and renewable energy development is particularly evident among low-income developing countries. Furthermore, dynamic panel threshold modeling identifies significant threshold values. Specifically, when regulatory quality exceeds −1.060, the association between climate finance and renewable energy development becomes positive; and when trade openness exceeds the threshold value, the positive association between climate finance and renewable energy becomes stronger. Therefore, improving regulatory quality and facilitating trade openness may create more favorable conditions under which climate finance is more strongly associated with renewable energy development.

Title: Automakers' electrification and R&D strategies under the dual-credit policy
Authors: Linyang Sun, Yuyin Yi

Title: Electricity market structure and consequences for wind and solar uptake in the EU-27
Authors: Jonas Grafström, Daniel Halvarsson, Theo Herold, Nadja Vinberg
Abstract: This paper examines whether concentration in electricity generation affects the deployment of wind and solar capacity across the 27 European Union member states over 2000–2022. Market concentration is measured by the generation share of the largest electricity producer, and wind and solar deployment is measured as installed wind and solar capacity relative to total national electricity capacity. Using a country-level panel and dynamic estimation methods that account for persistence, unobserved heterogeneity, and reverse causality—including fixed-effects OLS and Arellano–Bond GMM estimators with lagged concentration as an internal instrument—the analysis finds no systematic relationship between market concentration and subsequent wind or solar deployment. The result is robust across alternative concentration and outcome measures, bias-corrected dynamic panel estimators, balanced samples, region-specific linear time trends and heterogeneity analyses across regions, transition stages, energy-system characteristics, and policy regimes. The findings suggest that within the EU institutional setting, market concentration per se is not a first-order constraint on renewable uptake; instead, deployment is primarily driven by policy settings and the path dependence inherent in installed capacity.

Title: Regulatory architecture and shipowner investment response under overlapping carbon-pricing regimes
Authors: Angelica Kemene, Vangelis Tsioumas
Abstract: Maritime transport, responsible for roughly 3% of global greenhouse gas emissions, faces overlapping carbon-pricing regulation as the EU Emissions Trading System extends to shipping and the International Maritime Organization develops a prospective Net-Zero Framework with tradeable Remedial Units. This raises a central question: whether instrument interaction, rather than the stringency of any one measure, changes firm-level investment when carbon prices are held fixed, and how it shapes investment policy and the value of flexibility under uncertainty. We develop a correlated three-factor real-options framework using Longstaff–Schwartz continuation-value estimation with independent validation and test-sample policy evaluation, jointly modelling freight, fuel and carbon prices with calibrated cross-correlations and a Poisson hazard model for regulatory activation. We apply it to a Long Range 2 product tanker across four regimes: EU ETS phase-in, sustained regional fragmentation, and EU ETS plus IMO under netted or stacked interaction rules. Three findings emerge. First, regulatory architecture is economically material: netted versus stacked rules shift strategy NPVs by approximately $1 million at unchanged carbon prices. Second, the efficiency-first ranking is preserved across all regimes, including fragmentation where effective carbon exposure nearly doubles. Third, direct fuel-price support of about $200–300 per tonne substantially improves staged alternative-fuel pathways but does not eliminate the structural advantage of low-CAPEX efficiency retrofits, indicating that per-tonne support narrows but does not close the remaining economic gap. Results are robust across sixteen sensitivity dimensions and Capesize and feeder cross-segment checks.

Title: Which carbon policies redirect innovation? Comparative evidence on policy instruments and policy mixes in China
Authors: Qiang Li, Lidong Chen, Wei Jin, Lin Zhang
Abstract: This paper examines how different carbon-transition policy instruments and policy mixes are associated with the direction of firm-level innovation in the presence of non-green technological lock-in. Using patent data for Chinese A-share listed firms from 2003 to 2021, we first document strong path dependence: firms with larger stocks of non-green patents are significantly more likely to produce further non-green patents than to shift toward green innovation. We then compare four policy instruments—carbon emissions trading, low-carbon city pilots, vertical environmental management reform, and green loan interest subsidies—within a unified empirical framework. The results reveal clear differences in conditional associations across instruments. Carbon emissions trading, low-carbon city pilots, and green loan interest subsidies are associated mainly with the redirection of inherited non-green capabilities toward green patenting, whereas vertical environmental management reform is the only instrument associated with both reduced non-green innovation persistence and stronger green redirection. Policy-mix results show that focused combinations are associated with more consistent redirection effects, while broad policy bundling provides no clear additional gain, suggesting that complementarity and coherence matter more than the sheer number of instruments. These findings highlight the importance of instrument design, policy complementarity, and cautious interpretation of comparative policy evidence in innovation-led decarbonization.

Title: Decomposing the pollution generation process: Who is to blame?
Authors: Aurélie Slechten, Barnabé Walheer
Abstract: We propose a production-theoretic decomposition of long-run changes in emissions per worker that explicitly models the pollution-generation process.Building on frontier-based productivity decompositions, we separate emissions changes into efficiency change, frontier-shift change, labor productivity growth, and capital-labor ratio increases.To account for heterogeneity across countries, we estimate group-specific nonparametric production frontiers and apply the decomposition to 89 countries over 1960-2019.Counterfactual distribution analysis suggests that frontier-shift components are quantitatively important for understanding the observed cross-country distribution of emissions per worker in the final period.At the country level, labor-productivity gains and the capital-labor ratio generally exerted upward pressure on emissions.Efficiency improvements played a secondary but still meaningful role, with many countries behaving as "followers": improving efficiency relative to the frontier without necessarily shifting the frontier itself.

Title: Expected revenue, risk, and grid impact of Bitcoin mining: A decision-theoretic perspective
Authors: Yuting Cai, Ruthav Sadali, Korok Ray, Chao Tian
Abstract: Most current assessments use ex post proxies that miss uncertainty and fail to consistently capture the rapid change in bitcoin mining. We introduce a unified, ex ante statistical model that derives expected return, downside risk, and upside potential profit from the first principles of mining: Each hash is a Bernoulli trial with a Bitcoin block difficulty-based success probability. The model yields closed-form expected revenue per hash-rate unit, risk metrics in different scenarios, and upside-profit probabilities for different fleet sizes. Empirical calibration closely matches previously reported observations, yielding a unified, faithful quantification across hardware, pools, and operating conditions. This foundation enables more reliable analysis of mining impacts and behavior.

Title: Banking on carbon: modeling intertemporal equilibrium in China's rate-based emissions trading system
Authors: Limin Du, Huiying Peng, Zheng Wang
Abstract: China's emissions trading system (ETS) is a key market-based strategy to meet its ambitious “dual-carbon” targets of peaking emissions and reaching neutrality. Unlike “cap-and-trade” markets that limit total pollution, China's “rate-based” system adjusts permits based on production intensity. To understand how this unique design and “allowance banking”—saving permits for future use—influence long-term stability, this paper develops a discrete-time equilibrium model for the power sector. Theoretically, we show that China's rate-based approach better balances industrial growth with emissions abatement than traditional caps. The numerical simulations show that, under the rate-based approach, allowance prices rise steadily, carbon emissions decline continuously, thermal power output contracts moderately, and trading volume exhibits an overall upward trend. These results remain robust across alternative discount-rate assumptions. A comparison between cap-and-trade and rate-based approach further reveals that, when cumulative allowance allocation is held constant across regulatory regimes, rate-based approach results in higher allowance prices and greater thermal power output in most periods. These findings clarify the dynamics of intensity-based markets, providing a vital roadmap for policymakers to manage price stability and ensure the market's long-term success.

Title: Oil price shocks and private equity versus unicorns: transmission channels and policy implications
Authors: Rayenda Khresna Brahmana, Adnan Aslam
Abstract: This study examines how oil price shocks (supply, demand, and risk) are transmitted to private markets (Private Equity and Unicorns), an area largely absent from the literature that has focused almost exclusively on public financial markets. To test the hypothesis, we utilize Morningstar private market indices, including developed market private equity and unicorn indices across Asia, Europe, the United Kingdom, the United States, India, and China, and apply vector autoregressions, Markov-switching models, and wavelet quantile methods. Overall, oil price shocks transmit asymmetrically across private market segments, with developed market private equity exhibiting systematic sensitivity while unicorn markets remain largely insulated. Results show that developed market private equity is systematically responsive across all three shock types: supply and demand shocks lower returns, while risk shocks deepen losses during crisis regimes, with transition probabilities confirming prolonged distress following supply disruptions. Impulse response functions confirm demand shocks produce the broadest immediate effects, while wavelet analysis reveals short-term vulnerabilities in unicorn markets that dissipate over longer horizons. Only China and US unicorns register partial sensitivity under supply shocks, suggesting that growth dynamics and appraisal-based valuation dampen oil shock transmission broadly. For practitioners, the findings indicate that oil shocks alter private equity risk premia but carry limited implications for unicorn assets, offering novel insights for asset allocation, diversification, and systemic risk monitoring.

Title: The dual burden of energy poverty and climate exposure
Authors: Yuetong Zhang
Abstract: Households in the United States face compounded risks when high energy burdens intersect with heightened exposure to climate extremes. This study introduces a methodological framework to systematically identify and analyze these dual-vulnerability households. Using the 2020 Residential Energy Consumption Survey (RECS) linked with high-resolution NASA Daymet climate data, I spatially match households to localized measures of extreme climates like heatwaves and cold spells. Geospatial hotspot analysis reveals regions where economic and climatic risks converge, while Local Linear Forest models are employed to identify the primary drivers of household energy expenditures. The results show that climate-related variables, such as extreme temperature events and degree days, together with housing characteristics, exhibit greater predictive importance on energy costs than income. Policy simulations of programs, including appliance upgrades, weatherization, smart home technologies, and financial assistance programs, show heterogeneous predicted outcomes across household types, with technology-based strategies associated with the largest predicted reductions in energy expenditures. These findings highlight the importance of regionally tailored, climate-responsive policies that integrate technical upgrades with socioeconomic support to enhance resilience among households at the intersection of energy poverty and climate risk.

Title: Demand effects and welfare properties of energy efficiency standards
Authors: Junichi Minagawa, Thorsten Upmann
Abstract: We investigate how a common energy efficiency improvement across multiple energy-using activities affects demand, energy use, and emissions within a standard consumer framework. In contrast to the traditional rebound literature, which focuses on a single good or service, our analysis captures both substitution and income effects across several energy-using activities. We derive decompositions for (i) total demand for energy-using activities, (ii) the associated total energy demand, and (iii) the resulting emissions. These decompositions reveal that efficiency gains may lead to unintended increases in energy use or emissions, depending on the preference structure and relative marginal emissions. Building on these results, we derive a rule for the optimal design of energy efficiency standards. In the representative household case, this rule implies that the regulated price of each energy-using activity should be proportional to its marginal emissions and the absolute value of its own-price elasticity. We extend the analysis to heterogeneous households and show how the rule generalizes under equity considerations and aggregate emissions constraints. Our results provide a theoretical foundation for designing sector-specific energy efficiency standards in line with environmental and distributional objectives.

Title: An explainable machine learning analysis of retail renewable premiums
Authors: Yufan Ji, Noah Dormady, Abdollah Shafieezadeh, Kathryn Diana, Matthew Hoyt, Alberto J. Lamadrid L., Samantha Fox
Abstract: Estimating the supplier’s premium on retail renewable energy is persistently challenging. 14 U.S. states and several international jurisdictions have implemented retail restructuring (i.e., ”retail choice”) through which consumers can shop for electricity supply from marketers. These marketers often offer plans with varying compositions of renewable energy supplied by renewable energy certificates (RECs). This study quantifies the renewable energy premium on residential electricity offers using comprehensive data from Ohio’s retail choice market (2014–2023). We develop an algorithm that matches renewable and non-renewable offers by the same supplier on the same day, with virtually identical offer details (e.g., maturity, monthly fee, termination fee) over 120,000 matched contracts. Using a gradient boosting model with SHAP (Shapley Additive Explanations), we characterize how observable contract features and wholesale market conditions (e.g., forward hub prices) on the renewable energy premium of renewable offers. On average, renewable contracts include a markup of 7.67% (price difference of 0.642 cents/kWh). However, results also indicate that longer contract maturities and higher early termination fees are associated with lower renewable energy premiums, suggesting that renewable premiums vary systematically across contract structures. Importantly, we find robust empirical evidence for the presence of a trigger price: when forward wholesale energy prices are below $47.9/MWh, marketers obtain renewable energy premiums through higher marginal prices. Above this trigger, marketers no longer obtain a higher premium on renewable offers and instead manipulate maturities and early termination fees. Policy implications for market design and societal environmental objectives are presented.

Title: Climate change and credit risk of rural financial institutions: Evidence from China
Authors: Peng Peng, Shuo Han, Bingbing Zhang
Abstract: Extreme precipitation, as a key climate physical risk, critically affects the credit risk of the financial system, particularly in vulnerable sectors. However, existing research pays insufficient attention to its micro-level transmission mechanisms and systemic spillover effects. Using meteorological observation data and financial data of rural financial institutions in China from 2010 to 2021, this paper systematically examines the impact of extreme precipitation on the credit risk of rural financial institutions and its transmission pathways. We find that extreme precipitation raises the credit risk level of rural financial institutions, with the core mechanisms being the reduction of agricultural output and losses in housing assets. Further supplementary analysis indicates that extreme precipitation events can amplify the risk interaction and spillover effects among different types of banks, with the risk linkage between rural commercial banks and city commercial banks being the most sensitive. These findings highlight the importance for financial institutions to conduct scenario analysis and stress testing, and provide micro-level evidence for building a climate-resilient financial system.

Title: Machine learning for detecting collusion and capacity withholding in wholesale electricity markets
Authors: Jeremy Proz, Martin Huber, Ivan Marin
Abstract: Collusion and capacity withholding in electricity wholesale markets are important mechanisms of market manipulation. This study applies a refined machine learning-based cartel detection algorithm to two cartel cases in the Italian electricity market and evaluates its out-of-sample performance. Specifically, we consider an ensemble machine learning method that uses statistical screens constructed from the offer price distribution as predictors for the incidence of collusion among electricity providers in specific regions. We propose novel screens related to the capacity-withholding behavior of electricity providers and find that including such screens derived from the day-ahead spot market as predictors can improve cartel detection. We find that, under complete cartels - where collusion in a tender presumably involves all suppliers - the method correctly classifies up to roughly 95% of tenders in our data as collusive or competitive, improving classification accuracy compared to using only previously available screens. However, when trained on larger datasets including non-cartel members and applying algorithms tailored to detect incomplete cartels, the previously existing screens are sufficient to achieve 98% accuracy, and the addition of our newly proposed capacity-withholding screens does not further improve performance. Overall, this study highlights the promising potential of supervised machine learning techniques for detecting and dismantling cartels in electricity markets.

Title: Private ownership and pricing: Evidence from the Swedish district heating sector
Authors: Erik Lundin
Abstract: I examine the pricing behavior of municipal and private firms in the unregulated Swedish district heating market, characterized by geographically bounded local monopoly networks. Nearly all firms employ two-part pricing. Conditional on exogenous cost factors, private ownership is associated with a fixed-fee premium equivalent to 6.5 percent of the municipal average total price. Consistent with standard monopoly theory, the price difference is concentrated in the fixed fee, while the estimated difference in the unit price is statistically insignificant. The estimated total-price premium is nevertheless smaller, because the point estimate for the unit price is negative. Further, there is suggestive evidence that foreign-owned private firms charge an additional fixed-fee premium relative to domestically owned private firms, although this estimate is less precise. A descriptive analysis of financial statements indicates that private firms report higher profit margins, despite municipal firms being legally required to operate in a business-like manner. These findings are consistent with private firms exercising more market power than public firms in this market, so that the resulting upward pressure on prices appears to outweigh any downward effects from the potential cost efficiencies associated with privatization.

Title: Trading off capacity factors, location, storage, access charges and curtailment for renewable electricity
Authors: David Newbery
Abstract: Variable renewable electricity (VRE, wind and solar PV) is typically located far from load centres. As marginal curtailment is 3+ times average curtailment, VRE curtailment rises rapidly, demanding costly transmission expansion. Efficiency requires trading-off curtailment to reduce transmission against the value of curtailed VRE. This article develops novel closed-form formulas for the efficient transmission expansion, renewables capacity and voluntary curtailment in a simplified model of distant VRE. Given VRE entry equilibrium in demand centres, the solutions depend only on cost and technology parameters. If local grid-connected storage covers most of its cost, co-located storage increases the profit of onshore wind, reducing optimal export capacity. Calibration for Scottish wind shows overhead lines have little effect on desirable levels of curtailment/congestion but proposed costly subsea links increase efficient curtailment to the point where most Scottish wind expansion becomes unprofitable.

Title: ESG as a mitigator of oil volatility risk
Authors: Ludovico Luce, Elias Demetriades, Alexandros Kontonikas, Athanasios Triantafyllou
Abstract: ESG activities are a forward-looking measure to prevent risks from negative externalities. Linking ESG scores with the crude oil market, we assess their mitigating effect on returns during periods of rising oil price volatility. We examine the interplay between ESG scores and crude oil volatility's impact on returns. Interestingly, this interaction transforms ESG into an insurance-like hedge, protecting returns as volatility increases. Notably, we identify a pivotal turning point at relatively low volatility levels. Below this threshold, ESG activities lack effectiveness, but when volatility surpasses it, their hedging power becomes pronounced. This effect intensifies as volatility rises, rewarding ESG leaders more significantly. Our sectoral and quantile analyses corroborate these findings. Overall, our findings support the role of ESG activities as a "safe haven" in times of financial turmoil, focusing its contribution to the interplay between ESG and oil volatility on periods of heightened uncertainty in the crude oil market.

Title: Coping collectively: Responses to natural disasters in Africa
Authors: Robert Mackay, Astghik Mavisakalyan, Yashar Tarverdi
Abstract: Natural disasters are occurring with increased frequency, significantly affecting the lives of those exposed. We study the coping responses to disasters, matching data on over 1000 disaster locations with individual-level survey data from over 175,000 individuals across 37 African countries in the period 2002-2015. Using a difference-in-differences strategy that exploits spatial and temporal distances to disaster events, we show that disaster exposure is associated with increased economic vulnerabilities. While government support could be critical under such circumstances, we document lower evaluations of government performance in disaster-affected areas. Our analysis of coping responses suggests that disaster-exposed individuals are more likely to contact leaders as a group and participate in community meetings. However, while we document shifts in political interests and democratic attitudes among disaster-exposed individuals, their individual political activism declines. We find considerable heterogeneity in these relationships across countries, suggesting that national context shapes how disasters influence citizen-state relations.

Title: Systematic risk spillovers of China's traditional energy sector: A digitalization perspective
Authors: Miaomiao Tao, David Roubaud
Abstract: China is currently undergoing a significant transformation in its energy sector, aiming to expand its renewable energy capacity while still relying on conventional fossil fuels. This transition is complicated by external shocks, including the COVID-19 pandemic and the Russia-Ukraine conflict, which impose additional operational and financial pressures on energy firms. In this study, we examine risk spillovers among China's traditional energy firms, with a particular focus on the role of digitalization in mitigating the spread of these risks. Our analysis, in particular, reveals that external events, such as the US shale crisis, global stock market downturns, the Russia-Ukraine conflict, and the COVID-19 pandemic, disproportionately affect China's conventional energy sector, exposing systemic vulnerabilities. Notably, the Russia-Ukraine crisis has influenced domestic risk dynamics, prompting provinces to strategically adjust their energy portfolios (by, for example, prioritizing renewable adoption). We find that firm-level digitalization can effectively curb outward risk spillovers, primarily by diversifying supply chain concentration and fostering technological innovation. However, disruptions associated with CPU events can undermine the protective effect of digitalization, thereby amplifying the transmission of risk across these traditional energy firms.

Title: A contingent behavior approach for estimating price elasticities
Authors: Richard T. Carson, Jiajun Lu, Thomas Sterner, Dale Whittington
Abstract: Abstract ​Analysis of many policy interventions depends on the availability of accurate estimates of price, income and other elasticities. Economists typically use revealed preference data to estimate these elasticities ex-post. We propose a simple survey-based contingent behavior approach for estimating ex-ante (expected) elasticities as well as their distributions in the population. Ex-ante and ex-post estimates of eleasticities may differ for legitimate reasons; both are relevant to policymakers. We illustrate this CB approach using data from seven Global South countries. Results show that it is possible to develop contemporaneous country-specific estimates of ex-ante elasticities quickly and inexpensively in data-poor environments. We also discuss how these ex-ante elasticities may inform policy acceptance.

Title: Editorial Board
The West-to-East Power Transmission project and corporate green productivity: Evidence from Chinese industrial enterprises
Authors: Li Xie, Zhisheng Huang
Abstract: Against the backdrop of advancing high-quality development and green transition, the construction of cross-regional power transmission projects has emerged as a pivotal initiative for fostering a green, low-carbon, and high-quality spatial pattern. This study focuses on Chinese industrial enterprises, treating the commissioning of the West-to-East Power Transmission (WEPT) project as a quasi-natural experiment of cross-regional power resource allocation. Employing a multi-period difference-in-differences (DID) model, we empirically investigate the mechanism by which cross-regional power resource allocation through the WEPT project affects enterprises' green productivity. The findings indicate that the WEPT project has a significant positive effect on enterprises' green productivity, primarily through improved efficiency in allocating green resources. This project alleviates the cost burden on enterprises by mitigating regional electricity price distortions and facilitating industrial agglomeration, thereby stimulating their investment in emission-reduction equipment and enhancing their green productivity. Meanwhile, the impact of the WEPT project on enterprises' green productivity is asymmetric: it primarily improves green productivity in power-importing regions, at the terminals of thermal power transmission lines, and among state-owned and small- and medium-sized enterprises. Furthermore, the capacity enhancement enabled by the technological iteration of the WEPT project and the expansion of the layout scope facilitated by its technological selection have notably propelled the green transformation and development of enterprises. This driving effect not only fosters enterprises' green development through energy-saving effects but also operates via emission-reduction effects, with the latter being more prominent.

Title: Oil news shocks and the U.S. consumer sentiment and spending
Authors: Zeina Alsalman
Abstract: This paper examines the impact of oil news shocks on U.S. consumer sentiment and spending using a monthly Proxy-VAR model estimated over 1978:1–2019:12. Oil news shocks generate a delayed fall in both the Index of Consumer Sentiment (ICS) and Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE), with declines emerging about one year after the shock. ICS sub-indices and related measures reveal persistent falls in expectations about personal finances, business conditions, and buying conditions, and a significant increase in inflation expectations. Disaggregated PCE responses show that durable-goods spending increases briefly, consistent with intertemporal substitution, before turning negative, while nondurables, services, and energy-related spending fall immediately and persistently. Extending the sample through 2024 yields generally similar responses, though household behavior shows a short-lived improvement. A forecast-error variance decomposition indicates that oil news shocks explain meaningful medium- and long-horizon variation in inflation expectations, sentiment toward major purchases, and major consumption components, underscoring their role as expectation-driven disturbances.

Title: Does real-time pricing deliver lower carbon emissions?
Authors: Magdalena Strasburger, Tracey Dodd, Tim Nelson
Abstract: This study examines the relationship between household electricity consumption and carbon (CO₂) emissions costed in terms of real-time pricing (RTP) versus a static tariff. The analysis is based on 57 million hourly observations taken between February 2024 and January 2025 from 10,751 German households, each equipped with some kind of energy management system and most with a home battery. Overall, we find that RTP customers do not consume electricity with lower CO₂ intensity than customers on static tariff. In fact, both groups have negative price coefficients, but the effect is much stronger for RTP households. Customers on a static tariff show little response to price changes, whereas RTP customers reduce their consumption much more noticeably when prices rise. However, static customers have slightly lower CO₂ emissions per unit. Hence, while RTP might encourage customers to shift their usage patterns to lower-priced periods, this does not necessarily align with periods of low CO₂ output. Our results also illustrate that batteries and electric-vehicle chargers are critical enablers of load shifting. Yet, even with these technologies, the times at which people use electricity rarely coincides with the cleanest grid hours. These findings challenge the assumption that RTP inherently reduces emissions without also installing ancillary physical technologies, like batteries. Most importantly, this research shows the importance of integrating real-time carbon intensity signals with pricing and better access to enabling technologies to align electricity use with cleaner grid conditions.

Title: Corrigendum to “The impact of financial stress, governance, and geopolitics on Europe's energy transition mineral trade” [Energy Economics, 146 (2025) 108523].
Authors: Oleg Mariev, Md. Monirul Islam
Abstract: A brief replication package was originally submitted with the paper. It has now been expanded to enable exact reproduction of the results, as verified by the authors and the editor-in-chief. The authors gratefully acknowledge the journal's initiative in encouraging authors to provide detailed replication packages.Supplementary materialSupplementary data to this article can be found online at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eneco.2026.109533.

Title: From green electricity to green fertilizer: Economic and environmental benefits of ammonia diversified utilization in agricultural parks hybrid renewable energy systems
Authors: Sijie Wu, Lihui Zhang, Songrui Li, Dandan Pan, Shaoze Li
Abstract: Rural hybrid renewable energy systems (RHRES) are the primary means of achieving a low-carbon energy transition in rural areas. However, existing RHRES have paid insufficient attention to the application potential of green ammonia, failing to fully leverage its green value in energy utilization and agricultural production. To address this, we constructed an agricultural park hybrid renewable energy system (APHRES) based on the diverse synergistic utilization of green ammonia. It employs Power-to-Ammonia to convert surplus green electricity into green ammonia, which is then used for seasonal energy storage (SES), zero-carbon power generation, and green fertilizer production, thereby expanding the application scenarios of green ammonia in rural areas. We constructed a low-carbon operation optimization model for APHRES based on cost minimization, incorporating energy supply and demand fluctuations observed on typical days across seasons, and conducted simulation analysis using seven progressive scenarios. The results indicate that: (1) integrating biogas power generation with bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS) improves economic efficiency and carbon reduction, compared with the baseline scenario, total costs are reduced by 27.90%, and carbon emissions decreased by 37.75%; (2) the green ammonia-driven green fertilizer pathway can replace traditional high-carbon fertilizers and increase energy sales revenue by an additional 17.14%; (3) ammonia use in SES mitigates mismatches between renewable energy fluctuations and seasonal agricultural loads, enhancing standalone system operation; and (4) carbon market mechanisms, green product prices, equipment investment costs, and green ammonia subsidies are critical determinants of APHRES adoption and the market competitiveness of green ammonia and green fertilizers. This study proposes a sustainable production model for agricultural parks that combines green electricity, green ammonia, and green fertilizers, offering a replicable and innovative pathway for the low-carbon transition of rural energy.

Title: Strategic bid response under automated market power mitigation in electricity markets
Authors: Chiara Fusar Bassini, Jacqueline Adelowo, Priya L. Donti, Lynn H. Kaack
Abstract: In auction markets that are prone to market power abuse, preventive mitigation of bid prices can be applied through automated mitigation procedures (AMP). Despite the widespread application of AMP in US electricity markets, there exists scarce evidence on how firms strategically react to such price-cap-and-penalty regulation: when the price cap rarely leads to penalty mitigation, it is difficult to distinguish whether AMP are an effective deterrent or simply too lax. We investigate their impact on the bids of generation firms, using 2019 data from the New York and New England electricity markets (NYISO, ISO-NE). We employ a regression discontinuity design, which exploits the fact that the price cap with penalty is only activated when a structural index (e.g., congestion, pivotality) exceeds a certain cutoff. By estimating the Local Average Treatment Effect (LATE) of screening activation, we can causally identify successful deterrence of anti-competitive behavior. Around 30-40% of the analyzed bidders per market exhibit a significant strategic response - corresponding to a decrease in maximum bid prices of 4-10 $/MWh to avoid the penalty. However, there is significant heterogeneity between firms, and the regulatory impact on the overall market is not statistically detectable, suggesting lax mitigation thresholds. Using a merit-order simulation, we estimate the welfare impact of more stringent thresholds to lie between 350 and 980 thousand dollars of increased buyer surplus per mitigated hour, with the associated number of mitigated hours being below 33 hours/year. Our results motivate the empirical calibration of mitigation thresholds to improve the efficiency of AMP regulation.

Title: Electrification's role in carbon mitigation: Heterogeneous, dynamic, and threshold effects across nations
Authors: Hongliang Wu, Zheng Li, Heather Zhang
Abstract: Electrification is widely regarded as a key pathway toward deep decarbonization, yet its complex effects on carbon emission intensity across countries remain insufficiently understood. Using panel data from 49 countries over 1995–2020, this study investigates the dynamic, heterogeneous, and nonlinear effects of electrification on national carbon emission intensity. We combine a dynamic common correlated effects estimator with panel quantile and threshold regressions to account for global common shocks, cross-sectional dependence, and slope heterogeneity. The results indicate that, on average, electrification reduces carbon emission intensity, with stronger effects among countries at lower quantiles of the carbon-intensity distribution. We also identify a threshold effect whereby carbon emission intensity initially rises with electrification but declines once electrification exceeds a critical threshold. These findings suggest that electrification can reduce carbon emission intensity, but its effectiveness varies across stages of electrification and depends on country-specific structural conditions.

Title: The impact of green intelligence and the role of government subsidies under the dual carbon policy in China
Authors: Wei Wang, Weixian Wei
Abstract: This paper examines the macroeconomic, environmental, and welfare implications of China’s dual-carbon control policy, combining carbon emission intensity control and emission cap policies, and its interaction with the green-intelligent transformation of industrial production, constructing a dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) model that incorporates carbon regulation, heterogeneous subsidy policies, and independent (Formula presented) by green-intelligent (GI) producers to identify optimal subsidy responses under varying GI output shares. We find that both regulatory policies effectively reduce carbon emissions, but intensity control generates greater macroeconomic disruption, whereas cap control delivers more stable outcomes with lower inflation. When carbon revenue is redistributed, emission reduction subsidies offset the medium- and long-term output contraction, while GI technology (Formula presented) subsidies sustain long-term growth through technology spillovers whose strength rises in the GI output share. China-specific simulations for 2023–2035, calibrated to the country’s phased dual control trajectory, confirm that GI technology (Formula presented) subsidies are the preferred instrument, expanding green-intelligent output by 5.51% and total output by 2.25% relative to a no-subsidy baseline, whereas emission reduction subsidies trigger an endogenous carbon price spiral that depresses consumption by approximately 5.54% by 2035 Q4. Welfare analysis further reveals that layering subsidies on top of carbon regulation generates losses rather than gains, consistent with Tinbergen’s instrument-target principle, but these losses are small relative to the structural welfare gains from green-intelligent transformation: a rise in the GI output share from 0.304 to 0.45 improves welfare by approximately 28.50%. We further demonstrate that a fixed carbon price stabilizes the transition from intensity-based to cap-based regulation by anchoring low-carbon investment, moderating inflation, and smoothing macroeconomic adjustment, functioning as a complementary institutional arrangement that balances emission reduction goals with stable economic operation.

Title: Restoring price signals in electricity markets: A rule-based alternative to cost-plus regulation
Authors: Erkan Erdogdu
Abstract: Electricity tariff setting in emerging economies often faces a governance trilemma between cost recovery, macroeconomic stability, and political acceptability. This paper develops and evaluates a transparent, rule-based tariff mechanism as an alternative to discretionary, audit-centered regulation. Using Turkiye as a case study for high-inflation and high-loss environments, we apply an Autoregressive Distributed Lag (ARDL) framework to examine whether residential electricity bills can be benchmarked against publicly observable cost drivers, specifically consumer price index (CPI) and wholesale market clearing prices (MCP). The empirical results indicate that the exchange rate does not enter the long-run tariff equation independently once wholesale market prices are included. Correlation and VIF diagnostics suggest that this reflects substantial collinearity among USD/TRY, CPI, and MCP, consistent with the interpretation that exchange-rate pass-through is largely embedded in wholesale market prices and broader inflationary dynamics. Residual diagnostics point to serial correlation, heteroskedasticity, and non-normality, especially after 2020. These patterns are consistent with delayed tariff adjustment and discretionary price smoothing. Building on the estimated relationship, the paper derives an illustrative rule-based benchmark that anchors regulated tariffs to observable macroeconomic and market variables and separates non-technical losses from standard tariff recovery. The proposed framework offers a replicable approach to tariff-rule design, showing how transparent indexation can improve policy discipline, reduce information asymmetry, and make subsidy choices more explicit in volatile electricity markets.

Title: Self-reliance of supply chain actors under carbon policy: The role of carbon credits
Authors: Yang Bai, Ziqi Wang
Abstract: Under the regulation of carbon policies, intending to enhance sales and mitigate the financial strain, certain Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) have introduced carbon credits as a strategic marketing approach. To analyze the influence of OEM-provided carbon credits under carbon policies, we constructed a supply chain comprising a supplier and an OEM. We then examined the impact of these credits under two carbon policies: cap-and-trade policy and carbon tax policy. In modeling our approach, we considered scenarios where the supplier and the OEM lead the supply chain. Under the cap-and-trade policy, we also factored in the government-mandated carbon emission quota size and the supplier's initial emission level. The content of our study is the compensating effect of carbon credit on the subject profit of the supply chain under the regulation of carbon policy. Our findings reveal that the supplier might adopt varying strategies to safeguard their profitability as the carbon abatement cost coefficient escalates, including reducing wholesale prices to attract consumers. This approach also poses the risk of declining market demand and losses to OEM's profits. Interestingly, a carbon trading price hike increases supplier production costs and may simultaneously prompt them to lower wholesale prices, benefiting OEM.

Title: Monetary policy rules and environmental fiscal policy in a two-sector DSGE model
Authors: Oliver Holtemöller, Alessandro Sardone
Abstract: This paper examines how environmental externalities and fiscal policies aimed at reducing emissions affect the conduct of monetary policy in a two-sector (clean and dirty) environmental dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (E-DSGE) model. We analyze the response of monetary policy to sector-specific inflationary shocks under different environmental policy regimes and compare the performance of standard and non-standard monetary policy rules. In our framework, while the sectors are symmetric in terms of technology and nominal price rigidity, environmental fiscal policies -- such as carbon taxes or emission caps that affect only the dirty sector -- generate relative price distortions. Our findings highlight three key results. First, environmental policies introduce distortions in relative prices, altering the conduct of (Ramsey) optimal monetary policy. Second, a non-standard monetary rule targeting sector-specific inflation mitigates output, inflation, and emissions volatility more effectively. Third, this non-standard rule improves welfare across all environmental policy scenarios but leads to higher emissions, except under a cap policy, where emissions remain fixed by design. These findings underscore the critical role of policy-induced price asymmetries, besides structural ones, in shaping monetary policy responses, and reveal the complex interplay between monetary and environmental fiscal policies along with the trade-offs in designing optimal policy frameworks.

Title: Artificial intelligence and the energy trilemma: A general-purpose technology perspective
Authors: Eduardo Andres Pardo-Piñashca, Muhammad Shahbaz, Ioannis Kyriakou, Shoh-Jakhon Khamdamov
Abstract: As the world transitions toward cleaner energy systems, balancing energy security, energy equity, and environmental sustainability has become a major challenge in energy policy. These three often conflicting objectives reflect the energy trilemma, a fundamental concept for understanding the trade-offs involved in achieving the Sustainable Development Goals. Scholars have raised awareness of the potential of artificial intelligence to address energy transition challenges. However, its contribution to the trilemma remains inconclusive. Using panel data from 68 countries over 2002 to 2022, our results suggest that artificial intelligence improves the energy trilemma index. However, this aggregate improvement masks important heterogeneity across its dimensions. While artificial intelligence enhances energy security and environmental sustainability, it has a negative effect on energy equity, revealing asymmetric trade-offs. Drawing on the General-Purpose Technology (GPT) framework, a mechanism analysis reveals that artificial intelligence influences the trilemma index via energy efficiency, green technology innovation, and industrial structure upgrading. These results align with the three defining characteristics of AI as a GPT: continuous improvement, fostering complementary innovation, and pervasiveness. Furthermore, the effect of artificial intelligence on the trilemma index is non-linear under different levels of governance effectiveness and investment liberalization. In particular, weak governance effectiveness generates unintended consequences, leading AI to exert a negative effect on the trilemma index. Moreover, artificial intelligence contributes most strongly to improving the trilemma index under moderate levels of investment liberalization. Overall, these findings have important policy implications for addressing the energy trilemma by integrating artificial intelligence into energy systems.

Title: The impact of environmental regulation on clean innovation: Are there crowding out effects?
Authors: Nicola Benatti, Martin Groiss, Petra Kelly, Paloma Lopez-Garcia
Abstract: We examine the extent to which environmental regulation affects innovation and which policy types provide the strongest incentives to innovate. Using a local projection framework, we estimate the regulatory impact on patenting activity over a five-year horizon. As a proxy for environmental policy exposure, we estimate firm-level greenhouse gas emissions using a machine learning algorithm. At the country-level, policy tightening is largely associated with no statistically significant change in environmental technology innovation. At the firm-level, however, environmental policy tightening leads to higher innovation activity in technologies mitigating climate change, while the effect on innovation in other technologies is muted. This suggests that environmental regulation does not lead to a crowding-out of non-clean innovations. The policy type matters, as increasing the stringency of technology support policies and non-market based policies leads to increases in clean technology patenting, while we do not find a statistically significant impact of market-based policies.

Title: Grid connection costs as a barrier to new generation: Evidence from PJM and implications for transmission policy
Authors: Sarah Johnston, Yifei Liu, Chenyu Yang
Abstract: Meeting projected growth in electricity demand and climate goals will require building new electricity generators. The grid connection process is seen as a key constraint on this development. We collect new data on grid connection costs for PJM, the largest regional grid operator in the United States. We geographically match these costs to transmission spending to study their determinants. Using regression analysis, we find that these costs, and especially the network upgrade portion, are difficult to predict: generators with similar characteristics can have very different costs. We also find that planned generators with high network upgrade costs are much more likely to be canceled. Finally, prior transmission spending by the grid operator is associated with lower network upgrade costs for connecting generators. These findings emphasize the critical role of transmission capacity in expanding electricity generation capacity.

Title: The natural level of oil prices
Authors: Daniel Cuzzi, João Victor Issler
Abstract: This paper makes two original contributions. First, it introduces the concept of the natural level of oil prices, defined as the real price consistent with long-run supply and demand fundamentals in the absence of transitory shocks. Based on a cointegration framework linking oil prices to global industrial production, OPEC production, and non-OPEC production, the natural level provides a long-run anchor for oil prices, distinguishing temporary dislocations from permanent changes in oil markets.Second, splitting oil production between OPEC and non-OPEC producers in cointegration analysis is essential for identifying the natural level of oil prices, since their respective long-run impact on oil prices is not homogeneous.Empirical evidence indicates that transitory deviations from the natural level typically dissipate within 18–24 months. When we evaluate the out-of-sample forecasting performance of the proposed framework against the random walk, Hodrick–Prescott and Hamilton filters, and futures prices, the cointegration-based error-correction model consistently delivers the most accurate medium-term forecasts, reducing RMSE and MAE by 13%–22% relative to the random walk at 12–24-month horizons. We also derive a tractable decomposition of the oil risk premium as a function of the gap between observed and natural prices, showing how the natural level shapes expectations through the futures term structure.The proposed framework helps policymakers to distinguish persistent from transitory oil-price movements. It also provides investors and energy-market firms with a benchmark for assessing commodity-price risks, investment decisions, and long-term capital planning.

Title: Energy flexibility procurement strategy in competitive demand response markets: Dual-channel supply chain perspective
Authors: Xinyue Fei, Cheng Lyu, Yibo Ding
Abstract: The Demand Response (DR) market is crucial for smart grids to procure energy flexibility, thereby achieving supply–demand balance. This paper establishes a game-theoretic framework for dual-channel flexibility procurement in the DR market, where a grid operator (GO) procures load flexibility from energy consumers (ECs) both directly (the direct channel) and through the service provider (SP) (the wholesale channel). We examine the strategic interaction between the two channels and show that introducing the direct channel can mitigate double marginalization in the incumbent wholesale channel, thereby improving total channel surplus. Under certain channel cost conditions, the direct channel even benefits its competitor, the SP. We also unravel the strategic role of the direct channel as a credible threat: when channel costs are moderate, it disciplines the SP’s behaviors even though it is inactive. The equilibrium is further validated in a case study. The results show that dual-channel procurement expands the DR market by over 60% when channel costs are low, and can increase the SP profits by 28%, and improve the social welfare at a probability of 54.41%.

Title: Climate justice: Historical accountability vs. international Paretianism
Authors: Hyunwoo Hong, Biung-Ghi Ju
Abstract: We examine two principles of allocative justice in the climate agreement - historical accountability (Neumayer, 2000) and international Paretianism, IP (Posner and Weisbach, 2010). The former requires that a country’s emissions rights be limited by its historical (emissions) debt. The latter is forward-looking and requires that the agreement should not make any country worse off. The international protocols satisfying historical accountability impose drastically greater burdens on advanced countries in Europe and North America than the Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement. Interestingly, the protocol supported by IP, despite being forward-looking and supposedly more favorable to advanced countries, also demands significant emissions reductions from them—often even more than the equal per capita allocation. This finding counters Posner and Weisbach’s earlier IP-based argument against the Kyoto Protocol (and the equal per capita rule).

Title: Oil shocks & suicide
Authors: Chandler Hubbard, Alexander James, Makenzi Scott
Abstract: We estimate the effect of positive and negative oil shocks on suicide. Using restricted-use, U.S. state-level mortality data, we find that negative shocks increase suicide risk and that positive ones have little effect. Baseline estimates indicate that from 2015 to 2020, the oil bust raised the average suicide rate in the most oil-rich states by roughly 13%. Exploring sources of heterogeneity, effects are largely driven by men and people without college degrees. Results are robust to various modeling decisions and assumptions and are not easily explained by compositional changes. Implications are discussed, especially as they relate to the clean-energy transition and the “resource curse.”

Title: Public data openness and the greening of firms’ energy consumption mix: evidence from China
Authors: Jing Liu, Mingwei Song, Tao Qiao, Qinlin Gong
Abstract: Public data openness has become an increasingly important element of digital governance, yet its implications for firms' energy use remain underexplored. Using a panel of Chinese publicly listed manufacturing firms located in 289 prefecture-level cities from 2011 to 2022, this study examines whether the launch of municipal public data platforms promotes the greening of firms' energy consumption mix. We employ a staggered difference-in-differences design with firm and year fixed effects. The results show that public data openness significantly improves the greenness of firms' energy consumption mix. Subsample analyses yield larger point estimates for firms in cities with high-quality public data openness, for state-owned enterprises, and for firms located in peripheral and non-resource-based cities. Moderation analyses indicate that government environmental policy attention and public environmental concern strengthen this relationship. Exploratory channel analyses provide suggestive evidence that public data openness may promote a greener energy consumption mix by increasing both the output and quality of green technology innovation and by promoting firms' digital transformation. These findings highlight how public data openness can support firms' transition toward cleaner energy use through the joint roles of policy signaling and data provision. They also offer policy insights for developing economies seeking to align digital governance with green-transition objectives, while recognizing that the broader applicability of the findings depends on institutional and developmental conditions.

Title: How does the renewable energy transition affect energy security and equity? Diverging effects in developing and developed countries
Authors: Yiwei Ren, Xunhuan Li, Siyou Xia
Abstract: This study investigates how the renewable energy transition differentially affects energy equity and security in developed versus developing countries. Using two-way fixed effects models and instrumental variable-generalized method of moments (IV-GMM) estimation with panel data for 65 countries over 2000–2023, we analyze the impact of power generation through renewables on five key indicators of energy equity and security. We find that power generation through renewables increases residential electricity prices and reduces electricity self-sufficiency in developed countries, but improves electricity access rates, reduces urban-rural access disparities, lowers residential electricity prices, and enhances energy self-sufficiency in developing countries. Mechanism analysis reveals that these diverging effects operate through distinct transmission channels: intermittency challenges and stranded asset problems in developed countries versus the diversification of power generation in developing countries. Our results suggest that the renewable energy transition weakens energy security and equity in developed countries but enhances energy security and equity in developing countries. This study contributes to the academic debate on the impact of the renewable energy transition on energy security and equity and calls for differentiated policies to ensure a sustainable, reliable, and just energy transition across the world.

Title: What does ETS do to real-side production activity? Firm-level evidence from Korea
Authors: Jinhyeok Yang
Abstract: This study examines the effects of Korea’s Emissions Trading Scheme (K-ETS) on real-side production activity in the manufacturing sector, using firm-level panel data from Statistics Korea’s Mining and Manufacturing Survey and a Difference-in-Differences design. It finds that K-ETS did not significantly affect the amount of value added generated by covered firms, but was accompanied by declines in both gross output and production costs during the first phase, suggesting a temporary scale-down in their production activity. Sectoral analysis reveals that the scale-down was more persistent in a few high-emission sectors. Covered firms also increased the share of electricity in their energy mix, although this adjustment was pronounced in the low-emission sector and limited in high-emission sectors. No consistent evidence of improved production efficiency was found, and employment effects were also statistically insignificant across sectors. These findings suggest that firms’ real-side adjustments to K-ETS were temporary in manufacturing as a whole, but more persistent in a few high-emission sectors. This raises concerns about long-term competitiveness in those sectors and suggests the importance of complementary support measures under a common ETS price signal.

Title: Resilience planning for power systems under deep climate uncertainty
Authors: Jiarui Wang, Junqi Liu, Lei Zhu, Gang He
Abstract: The rising frequency and intensity of extreme weather events introduce deep climate uncertainties that fundamentally challenge the resilience of urban power systems. Conventional deterministic planning approaches are ill-suited to capture such uncertainties, often leading to maladaptive investments and system vulnerabilities. We develop a data-driven robust planning framework to cope with climate uncertainties in power system. Specifically, a hybrid framework combining a Graph Neural Network and a Conditional Generative Adversarial Network (GNN-cGAN) is utilized to capture the spatiotemporal couplings of multiple meteorological variables, which provides a more realistic characterization of deep climate uncertainties and compound extreme events. According to the Minimax Regret (MMR) criterion, a two-stage robust planning model is proposed to balance economic efficiency with extreme climate resilience, which can effectively mitigates the excessive conservatism and prohibitive investment premiums of traditional robust optimization. Applied to Lvliang City, China, the results demonstrate that the proposed approach improves system resilience by avoiding investment lock-in and reducing the risk of performance degradation under extreme conditions. Compared to conventional planning methods, the framework achieves a more balanced trade-off between economic efficiency and climate adaptability.

Title: Climate policy diffusion across US states
Authors: Mitali Das, Manuel Linsenmeier, Gregor Schwerhoff
Abstract: Climate policy at the subnational level is sometimes framed as counterproductive because climate change is considered a collective action problem that can best be addressed in a coalition that should be as large as possible. Using comprehensive data from US states on climate policy and policy outcomes, we show that state-level policy is effective in accelerating the adoption of solar energy. Crucially, however, state policies also have positive spillovers to other states, making it more likely that neighboring states adopt climate policy as well. By proportionally attributing the spillover effects, we find that many US states achieve more climate benefits through the spillovers to other states than within their own jurisdiction. In a further step, we distinguish between climate policies in the energy sector and policies targeting either other sectors or greenhouse gas emission (GHG) reductions in general. We find that climate policies in the energy sector are distinct from other climate policies in two ways: They have a significant effect on solar capacity growth and diffuse more broadly.

Title: From emission trap to mitigation dividend: The nonlinear impact and mechanisms of rural infrastructure on agricultural carbon emissions in China
Authors: Yonghao Hu, Xiang Li, Xiaoxiao Li, Kunyang Zhang, Peirun Li, Laping Wu, Nanyan Hu
Abstract: Balancing agricultural carbon mitigation with food security has become a major challenge in the pursuit of global carbon neutrality. Rural infrastructure is a key form of public capital, yet its environmental impact remains unclear. Using provincial panel data from China covering the period 2005–2023, this study examines the impact of rural infrastructure on agricultural carbon emissions (ACE) and explores the underlying mechanisms. The analysis employs fixed-effects, instrumental variable, and spatial Durbin models. ACE follows an inverted U-shaped trajectory, peaking in 2015, while rural infrastructure exhibits a similar nonlinear effect. In the early stage, infrastructure increases emissions by expanding production scale and intensifying input use. As infrastructure develops, it reduces emissions through green technological progress. Mechanism analysis shows that infrastructure initially raises emissions by increasing cropping intensity, fertilizer use, and mechanization, but gradually promotes emission reduction by facilitating the adoption of water-saving irrigation. Technological progress thus becomes the dominant force driving transition beyond the environmental turning point. The effects of infrastructure vary across components. Water infrastructure shows a nonlinear transition. Electricity infrastructure supports emission reduction. Transport infrastructure tends to increase emissions.
