Infrastructure also generates spatial spillovers, with indirect effects exceeding direct effects. Substantial regional heterogeneity is observed. Plain regions and major grain-producing areas reach the turning point earlier. Mountainous regions face a higher risk of emission lock-in. These findings suggest that infrastructure investment should follow a stage-specific strategy. Policies should prioritize the adoption and diffusion of green technologies while strengthening cross-regional coordination to achieve agricultural decarbonization without compromising food security.

Title: Foreign direct investment and greenhouse gas emissions: Evidence across income groups and technological contexts
Authors: Narek Mirzoyan, Jennifer Brodmann, Mahmoud Salari, Sunghoon Joo
Abstract: This paper examines the relationship between foreign direct investment (FDI) and greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions in middle- and high-income countries. Particular attention is paid to income-group heterogeneity and the context of green technology. Using an unbalanced panel of 74 countries from 1975 to 2021, we estimate static and dynamic panel data models. The static analysis includes pooled OLS, random effects and two-way fixed effects specifications, incorporating income group and FDI-patent interactions. To address dynamic persistence and potential endogeneity, we also employ one-step and two-step system GMM estimators with lagged dependent variables and income-specific FDI effects. The results suggest a generally positive association between FDI and GHG emissions, although the magnitude and statistical significance of this relationship vary across different models. Dynamic system GMM estimations provide further evidence of a positive association between FDI and emissions. In the main interaction specifications, estimated effects are somewhat larger for middle-income economies than for high-income ones, though this difference is not consistent across all specifications and should be interpreted as suggestive rather than conclusive. Analysis of disaggregated green patent categories reveals substantial technological heterogeneity. Some patent classes are associated with a weaker FDI–emissions relationship, whereas others appear to strengthen it. In contrast, aggregate patent activity shows either positive or statistically insignificant relationships with emissions, suggesting that broad patent measures may obscure important technology-specific effects. Overall, FDI does not automatically lead to environmental improvement. Its consequences appear to vary with income-related structural conditions and the technological orientation of the host economy. These findings support broad policy caution: FDI attraction strategies should be evaluated together with environmental monitoring, and green innovation should be assessed at a more disaggregated technological level.

Title: Thinking machines, shrinking footprints? The impact of Artificial Intelligence on energy consumption in regions
Authors: Robert Dehghan, Nils Grashof, Sebastian Schmidt, Alexander Kopka, Michael Woywode
Abstract: As Artificial Intelligence (AI) becomes more widespread, concerns about its environmental impact, particularly its energy demand, are growing. At the same time, AI is often regarded as a key driver of industrial optimisation and efficiency. This paper examines this tension by analysing the impact of AI adoption on regional industrial energy consumption in Germany between 2012 and 2023. To do so, we combine a novel web-based machine learning approach that identifies AI and sustainability adoption based on company websites with regional data on energy consumption, technological knowledge, and economic structures. Using a system GMM approach, our results show that regions with a higher rate of AI adoption have significantly lower levels of industrial energy consumption. However, this energy-saving effect has weakened over time, being more pronounced in the period 2012–2017 than in the period 2018–2023. The energy-saving effects are also more pronounced in regions where a higher proportion of firms, both large and small, adopt AI. Furthermore, although interaction terms between AI adoption and knowledge relatedness to AI and green technologies are not statistically significant on average, marginal effects analysis uncovers substantial heterogeneity. The energy-reducing impact of AI adoption becomes stronger and statistically significant only at higher levels of relatedness to AI and green technologies, with effects emerging earlier for green-related knowledge bases. Our findings offer a novel perspective on the role of AI in promoting sustainable industrial development. They also emphasise the importance of capturing both the usage and creation of digital technologies within regional innovation systems.

Title: Predicting energy ETF prices: The impact of Google Trends and investor attention
Authors: Zihui Xia, Xiaotao Zhang
Abstract: From the perspective of investor attention, this study constructs an attention indicator based on Google Trends (GT) data and employs three types of models—Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), Rotation Forest, and ARIMA—to forecast the prices of energy exchange-traded funds (ETFs), including clean energy (ICLN), upstream traditional energy (XOP), and the overall energy sector (XLE). Overall, the inclusion of GT data significantly enhances the predictive performance of the CNN model, particularly for clean energy ETFs, with the CNN also demonstrating strong stability, making it the most suitable model among those examined. Moreover, the study reveals a marginal effect of GT information volume on model performance: the CNN model exhibits improved forecasting accuracy as GT information increases, whereas the Rotation Forest model may be subject to an information “threshold effect.” These findings offer valuable insights for quantitative investment and policy formulation in the context of green finance.

Title: Evidence of firm-level pollution leakage resulting from China's 2013 Clean Air Plan
Authors: Chang Liu, Jingrong Wang, David M. Reiner
Abstract: Spatially differentiated environmental regulation can induce pollution leakage through intra-firm relocation of pollution-intensive activities to less-regulated regions. This mechanism remains underexplored, especially in developing countries, where data limitations make intra-firm relocation difficult to measure and existing investment-based proxies often miss expansions within existing subsidiaries. Using manually collected subsidiary-level investment data for 411 listed pollution-intensive firms in China and a difference-in-differences framework, we examine whether regionally differentiated regulation under the 2013 Clean Air Plan led to intra-firm investment reallocation consistent with production relocation and potential domestic pollution leakage. We find that regulated firms increased pollution-related investment in subsidiaries located in less-regulated areas following the policy, accompanied by declines in parent-firm output and rising PM₂.₅ concentrations around subsidiary locations. Adjustment patterns differ across regions: firms in the three key regions centered on Beijing, Shanghai, and Guangzhou reallocate investment from eastern regulated areas to distant western regions, mainly through new subsidiary entry, whereas firms in ten other major city clusters mainly expand existing subsidiaries located nearby. Reallocated investment is disproportionately directed toward regions with stronger agglomeration economies and transportation advantages rather than environmentally fragile areas. These findings suggest that investment flows offer a valuable lens for detecting potential pollution leakage and that unintended east-to-west transfers may undermine environmental gains, highlighting the need for stronger disclosure requirements and targeted pollution-control policies in recipient regions.

Title: Optimal climate and monetary–fiscal policies in a climate-DSGE framework
Authors: Lorenzo Forni, Mehrab Kiarsi
Abstract: This paper studies the optimal design of climate, fiscal, and monetary policies in response to climate-specific shocks within a climate-DSGE framework. We show that carbon taxes significantly mitigate the effects of climate shocks on output, consumption, and welfare, while optimal monetary policy is largely unaffected and fiscal policy adjusts via lower labor taxes. Extending the model with a richer climate module and abatement costs, we find that the assumed damage function is crucial: under a standard quadratic specification, climate policy has little effect on conventional macroeconomic shocks, but a highly convex, Weitzman-type damage function makes carbon taxation materially relevant. Accounting for climate fiscal outlays further raises optimal abatement and reduces emissions. Our results highlight the importance of integrating both macroeconomic and environmental considerations when designing policy.

Title: The shape of U — On the structure of utility from electric vehicle charging
Authors: Philipp Theile
Abstract: With the growing adoption of electric vehicles, understanding user charging behavior is increasingly important for informing operational, investment, and policy decisions regarding their integration into the power system. While utility functions are commonly used to describe user preferences in charging behavior models, most existing studies rely on formulations with limited theoretical consistency and empirical validation, potentially leading to biased expectations.This paper empirically compares different utility function specifications and examines their implications for charging behavior modeling and charging station profitability.I introduce a novel discrete choice model framework to efficiently estimate utility function parameters from revealed preference data. Using a dataset of observed charging sessions at public charging stations in Germany, the model identifies accurate utility functions, uncovers charging preferences, and simulates station segment viability.The results suggest that charging utility is non-linear: marginal utility decreases with charged energy and marginal disutility increases with charging duration. An interaction between energy and duration leads to higher marginal valuation of energy for longer charging durations. Stations profit from inelastic demand driven by users who highly value energy content, are less price sensitive, and engage in high-value activities at the charging location, such as in urban areas or traffic hubs.

Title: Has the U.S. strengthened the resilience of its lithium-ion battery supply chain?
Authors: Jianhao Mei, Di Wang
Abstract: The pandemic has exposed significant vulnerabilities within the U.S. supply chains. To enhance the resilience of lithium-ion battery supply chains, the Biden administration has implemented a series of policies. This study comprehensively examines the U.S. policy framework, which includes a domestic policy structure consisting of a “Vertical Policy Hierarchy-Cross-Cutting Strategies-Policy Instrument” model, international cooperation, and tariffs. It also provides a holistic depiction of the lithium-ion battery supply chain risk assessment matrix and conducts an in-depth analysis of both domestic production and international supply chains. Lastly, this study offers preliminary correlational evidence of the effectiveness of these policies in strengthening supply chain resilience. Key findings include: 1) the overall resilience of the U.S. lithium-ion battery supply chain has not substantially improved; 2) domestic investments and jobs have increased, yet demand gaps persist; 3) import diversification coexists with concentrated dependency on critical minerals, the reliance on China for upstream resources has decreased through friend-shoring, but downstream dependency has intensified, accompanied by declining HDI and EPI scores and elevated climate and conflict risks; 4) international cooperation has reduced disruption risks, but high tariffs have been positively correlated with import concentration, supply chain distance, and geopolitical risks, failing to resolve explicit and implicit dependencies on China.

Title: How demand-side climate policy shapes public low-carbon involvement willingness: Evidence from the carbon generalized system of preferences in China
Authors: Jing Zhou, Ting Yue, Ying Wang, Claire Murong Cui, Ruyin Long, Wanqi Ma, Shouyang Wang, Le Wen
Abstract: Public participation plays a central role in demand-side climate mitigation and the broader low-carbon transition. As an incentive-based voluntary policy designed to encourage individual carbon-reduction behaviors, the Carbon Generalized System of Preferences (CGSP) provides an important policy context for examining how demand-side climate policies shape public low-carbon involvement willingness. This study examines whether and how the CGSP policy affects public low-carbon involvement willingness (LIW) across Chinese cities. Using large-scale social media data from 267 cities over 2013–2023, we construct city-level indicators of LIW through a deep learning framework. These indicators are then incorporated into a multi-period difference-in-differences model to estimate the policy's causal effects. The results show that the CGSP policy significantly enhances both cognitive and behavioral dimensions of low-carbon involvement willingness, with a relatively stronger effect on behavioral involvement. The effects exhibit substantial heterogeneity across regions, infrastructure conditions, and levels of internet development, with stronger effects in cities characterized by better infrastructure and relatively better internet development. Further analysis indicates that government attention (GA) and digital inclusive finance (DIFI) serve as important institutional and market-based channels linking the policy to public low-carbon involvement willingness. Specifically, GA primarily operates through the cognitive channel by enhancing information dissemination, while DIFI supports both cognitive and behavioral involvement willingness by reducing participation barriers and facilitating access to low-carbon services. These findings provide empirical evidence on the role of demand-side climate policies in promoting public low-carbon involvement and offer policy implications for designing incentive-based low-carbon governance instruments.

Title: Bitcoin’s productivity trap
Authors: Maximilian Gill, Jona Stinner, Marcel Tyrell
Abstract: Input efficiency gains often decouple digital technologies from rising resource use as they scale. Does the same apply to Bitcoin’s resource-intensive Proof-of-Work (PoW) mechanism? This paper develops a formal framework to assess this question. Our results show that the efficiency effect does not occur. The reason is that the protocol embeds a perfectly competitive rent-seeking game with fixed output, placing Bitcoin in a productivity trap: efficiency gains expand resource use without increasing output. The mechanism is structural, as PoW computations serve solely as costly signals rather than productive output. Our model shows that efficiency gains from surplus renewable energy, while lowering CO 2emissions, induce additional mining activity which increases e-waste and may offset environmental benefits. A multilaterally implemented Pigouvian tax could correct these externalities without reducing network output, whereas unilateral taxation may exacerbate them through carbon leakage. This underscores both the theoretical possibility and the practical difficulty of achieving a “green Bitcoin.”

Title: Strengthening environmental policies to boost energy efficiency: A quantile and sectoral approach for European OECD countries
Authors: Guillaume Bourgeois, Camille Massié Gamard
Abstract: This study examines the impact of environmental policy stringency, measured by the OECD's Environmental Policy Stringency Index (EPSI), on energy efficiency progress, proxied by the ODEX, across 18 European OECD countries from 2000 to 2020. Using panel fixed effects quantile regressions and two instrumental variable methods to address reverse causality, we analyze how market-based (MB), non-market-based (NMB), and technology support (TS) instruments affect energy efficiency gains across quantiles, sectors, and time. We show that a one-unit increase in the EPSI corresponds to a 6.6-percentage point improvement in national energy efficiency. This effect remains significant when accounting for delayed effects through lagged policy specifications, although with a declining magnitude over time. The decomposition of the EPSI reveals heterogeneous dynamic responses across policy instruments. NMB policies are the most effective overall, especially in lagging economies, and display persistent effects over time. TS instruments exhibit similar patterns in these contexts. By contrast, MB instruments perform better in mature economies and mainly operate through short-term behavioral adjustments. Sectoral analyses show that NMB policies strongly impact the industrial sector, while MB and TS mechanisms have no significant sector-specific effects. Our findings highlight the need for tailored policy interventions to maximize energy efficiency gains. Policymakers should prioritize NMB measures ( e.g. , mandatory emission limits, standards on harmful substances), deploy MB mechanisms ( e.g. , carbon pricing, energy taxes) where market maturity allows, while maintaining support for TS instruments ( e.g. , research and development for green innovation) as part of a comprehensive policy mix.

Title: An empirical estimate of the electricity supply curve from market outcomes
Authors: Jorge Sánchez Canales, Alice Lixuan Xu, Chiara Fusar Bassini, Lynn H. Kaack, Lion Hirth
Abstract: Researchers and electricity sector practitioners frequently require the supply curve of electricity markets and the price elasticity of supply for purposes such as price forecasting, policy analyses or market power assessment. It is common practice to construct supply curves from engineering data such as installed capacity and fuel prices. In this study, we propose a data-driven methodology to estimate the supply curve of electricity market empirically, i.e. from observed prices and quantities without further modeling assumptions. Due to the massive swings in fuel prices during the European energy crisis, a central task is detecting periods of stable supply curves. To this end, we implement two alternative clustering methods, one based on the fundamental drivers of electricity supply and the other directly on observed market outcomes. We apply our methods to the German electricity market between 2019 and 2024. We find that both approaches identify almost identical regimes shifts, supporting the idea of stable supply regimes stemming from stable drivers. Supply conditions are often stable for extended periods, but evolved rapidly during the energy crisis, triggering a rapid succession of regimes. Fuel prices were the dominant drivers of regime shifts, while conventional plant availability and the nuclear phase-out play a comparatively minor role. Our approach produces empirical supply curves suitable for causal inference and counterfactual analysis of market outcomes.

Title: Climate risk meets machine learning: Forecasting energy stock index volatility
Authors: Xue Gong, Jiahao Peng, Xiaodan Li
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel climate risk indicator (CRI) constructed from “feed index” data and a comprehensive set of climate-related keywords. Employing the partial least squares method, the proposed CRI exhibits significant in- and out-of-sample predictive power for energy stock index realized volatility. Its forecasting accuracy outperforms a broad range of benchmarks, including CRIs derived from alternative machine learning techniques, established climate indices, and energy-market factors. The findings remain robust across a range of validation checks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the CRI’s predictive power for energy stock index volatility is consistent with transmission through investor sentiment, market turnover, and the leverage effect. Finally, we show that integrating climate-related information yields modest economical improvements in low-volatility regimes but does not reverse negative full-sample Sharpe ratios.

Title: What drives electric vehicle owners to choose official end-of-life battery recycling channels?
Authors: Lei Shi, Xinyan Wang, Meirong Guo
Abstract: A large number of retired automotive power batteries are flowing into informal recycling channels, posing new environmental governance challenges. There is an urgent need for consumer behavioral guidance measures to steer them toward active participation in formal recycling. However, existing research lacks studies on more flexible consumer-oriented policies. Therefore, this study conducted a micro-survey targeting electric vehicle owners in a typical Chinese city. Based on it, we empirically examined the impacts of various potential recycling policies and multi-dimensional factors on owners' willingness to choose recycling channels. The findings indicate that the current cash deduction recycling policy has a positive effect on owners' willingness, but its effectiveness is limited to younger and low-income groups. Adopting more flexible strategies such as cash rebate and credit reward can further broaden the policy's effectiveness. In addition, the price spread between formal and informal recycling channels has a significant negative impact on owners' choice willingness. Enhancing owners' hazard cognition of informal recycling and their understanding of recycling regulations and policies can effectively increase their willingness to choose formal channels. Based on the results, we recommend that the government implement differentiated subsidy pricing based on the residual value of recycled vehicles, strengthen education on the hazards of informal battery recycling, promote national recycling policies, and adopt multiple differentiated strategies for different population groups.

Title: Green bonds and the energy transition: From instrumental use to intrinsic value
Authors: Peng Zhou, Wenjie Ding, Khelifa Mazouz, Shijie Jin
Abstract: Using bibliometric techniques, we classify green bonds literature into three main clusters: (i) asset-pricing research examining green bonds' connectedness with other assets; (ii) corporate-finance studies on the determinants of green bond issuance; and (iii) corporate-finance research on their environmental effects, such as carbon-emission reductions and renewable-energy deployment. Early studies primarily focused on pricing dynamics and market connectedness, whereas recent research emphasizes the intrinsic environmental value of green bonds, particularly their role in financing renewable-energy projects and supporting climate-policy objectives. This review integrates these strands into a unified energy-finance framework. On the theoretical side, we map green bond studies along a spectrum from instrumental to intrinsic value. On the methodological side, we synthesize the principal identification strategies used to address endogeneity, a challenge central to establishing credible links between green-bond financing and energy-transition outcomes. Building on these foundations, we set out a future research agenda that highlights underexplored issues concerning cross-market dynamics during energy crises, the effectiveness of green bonds in accelerating decarbonization, and the policy implications for energy-market regulators. Taken together, our findings provide a structured foundation for advancing research on green bonds within energy economics and climate finance.

Title: Dynamic investment, subsidies, and welfare effects of rural rooftop photovoltaics: A bilateral decision analysis in rural China
Authors: Zenghui Chao, Wenhao Gu, Wenyu Fan, Zhenzhi Wang, Jun Zhang
Abstract: To address climate change and energy transition issues, China is actively promoting rooftop photovoltaics (PV) in rural areas through a firm-household collaboration project. Under this project, firms benefit from electricity sales generated from rooftop PV, and rural households benefit from rents that firms compensate for the roof occupation. This study develops a bilateral dynamic real option model to analyze the economic and policy drivers of rooftop PV adoption in rural China under this project. With survey data from Pingdingshan city of Henan province, we use empirical methods and simulations to evaluate this collaboration project and illustrate how government subsidy would play roles in PV promotion and green energy transition. We found rural households generally have high willingness to accept (WTA) for rooftop photovoltaic compensation, resulting in extremely low spontaneous participation rates without external incentives. Our simulation analyses indicate that subsidy policies serve as the primary driver for project participation by increasing households' expected net welfare, and can simultaneously drive a stepwise increase in firms' profits and environmental benefits. Finally, we further quantify the transmission mechanism of subsidies in the “firm-household” bilateral game, where firms with bargaining power strategically reduce rental prices, thereby capturing a portion of the policy benefits flowing to households, allowing firms to maximize their own profits while still elevating participation rates. This study deepens theoretical understanding of rural PV promotion under uncertainty and offers a quantitative basis for relevant energy and environmental policy design.

Title: Macroeconomic and social impacts of Nigeria's net-zero development pathways: A hybrid model analysis
Authors: Chukwumerije Okereke, Chukwuemeka Emenekwe, Uchenna Nnamani, Nnaemeka Emodi, Ogheneruona Diemuodeke, Kesiena Owebor, Bruno Michoud, Frédéric Ghersi
Abstract: This research explores the macroeconomic and social impacts of five energy-explicit development pathways for Nigeria's economy: Baseline (BAU), Current Policy Scenario (CPS), Gas Economy Scenario (GES), Renewable Energy Scenario (RES) aligned with Nigeria’s 2060 net-zero emissions pledge, and a RES variant with international support (RES+). The analysis leverages soft-linking of the top-down KLEM-NGA macroeconomic model and the bottom-up LEAP-NGA energy system model, utilizing a comprehensive energy-economy database including original input-output and energy balance tables. Under the RES scenario, achieving emissions reductions incurs a 3.5% GDP and 3.2% employment loss by 2060 compared to BAU, or a 4.5% GDP loss compared to GES, which fully utilizes gas reserves to fuel the domestic economy and sustain the trade balance. However, the RES+ scenario, augmented by international aid to bridge the investment gap between CPS and RES, results in GDP and employment performances comparable to GES while reducing emissions to 16 million tons of CO2 equivalent in 2060, versus 151 million tons under GES. This transition, conditional on international aid totaling 880 billion USD over 39 years—an average of 1.1% of Nigerian GDP annually from 2022 to 2060—could pivot Nigeria from a short-sighted gas economy towards a sustainable net-zero future.

Title: Subsidies, information, and energy-efficient cookstove adoption – A natural field experiment in rural Ethiopia
Authors: Mandy Malan, Maarten Voors, Jörg Ankel-Peters, Selam J. Seje, Lotte Heuberger, Dawud Seid, Abiyot Mitiku
Abstract: Energy-efficient biomass cookstoves are an important technology for nearly 3 billion people relying on biomass for cooking in the Global South. This paper assesses the price-responsiveness of stove demand and the role of information about health and economic benefits from stove usage. We evaluate a pilot program that randomized different subsidy schemes (no subsidy, 40%, 70%, and 100% subsidy) and information treatments on the benefits of these stoves across 292 Ethiopian villages. Unlike several previous willingness-to-pay studies we examine a take-it-or-leave-it approach in a natural setting. We observe that stove demand is highly price-sensitive: there is virtually no uptake in the no-subsidy group, irrespective of which information about benefits households received. Uptake increases considerably for households who received a high subsidy (70% or 100%). Adding information on economic benefits nearly doubles uptake when coupled with such high subsidies. Our results confirm the emerging picture in the literature suggesting that subsidization fosters adoption considerably.

Title: From disasters to volatility: Extreme climate events and European financial markets
Authors: Alessandra Canepa, Bogdan Dima, Ştefana Maria Dima
Abstract: This paper examines how climate-related risks shape the volatility dynamics of major European financial markets, with a particular focus on long-run volatility. We investigate whether climate-related risks translate into persistent financial uncertainty and why long-run volatility responses differ across markets. The analysis proceeds in two steps. In the first step, we use a double-asymmetric GARCH–MIDAS framework to test whether extreme weather events affect long-run volatility and whether the response is asymmetric between adverse (above-average) and mild (below-average) extreme realizations. We find that physical climate risk has non-linear and asymmetric effects on long-run financial volatility, with some markets exhibiting substantially greater sensitivity than others. To explain this heterogeneity, in the second step of the analysis we move from a time-series to a panel framework and incorporate climate transition risk alongside physical risk. To do so, we construct a long-run volatility measure from realised variance and relate it to transition and physical climate risk measures, allowing the effects to vary with energy structure, sectoral exposure, institutional capacity, and macro-financial conditions. The panel results indicate that transition risk acts as a source of long-horizon uncertainty, but its impact depends on structural characteristics. Fossil-fuel-dependent countries and highly exposed sectors experience stronger volatility responses, while markets with greater renewable energy penetration and stronger institutional capacity tend to absorb transition-related uncertainty more smoothly. Physical climate risk also affects long-run volatility but mostly when extreme weather coincides with elevated energy uncertainty or macroeconomic instability. Overall, our findings underscore that climate risk is neither uniformly destabilising nor fully neutralised in financial markets but instead depends on country-specific structural characteristics and state-dependent macroeconomic dynamics.

Title: The value of dispatchability and earnings-at-risk of electricity generators in the energy transition
Authors: Lin Han, Nino Kordzakhia, Stefan Trück
Abstract: Electricity markets are currently going through a period of substantial transformation from coal-fired power generation to an increasing share of renewable energy. Despite the environmental benefits of increased renewable energy in terms of CO2 emission savings, the intermittency of variable renewable energy (VRE) not only increases the volatility of the remaining generators’ revenues, but also indicates high uncertainty for investment in renewables. This paper examines dispatch-weighted prices (DWPs) and earnings-at-risk (EaR) for different generation technologies in the Australian National Electricity Market. We find that dispatchable generators such as hydro, natural gas and battery storage with controllable and flexible output achieve higher DWPs than less flexible generators such as coal fired power plants. They also achieve higher DWPs than VRE generators, i.e. solar and wind farms, which are non-dispatchable. Examining cashflow-based EaR measures, we further find very different risk profiles for different generation technologies. While dispatchable and flexible generators with stronger correlation with spot prices have generally higher upside potential of earnings compared to coal fired plants and VRE generators, their EaRs are also much higher, which indicates greater uncertainty in profits. Furthermore, the seasonal analysis suggests that the transition toward a renewable-dominated supply mix is making winter the season with the most volatile spot prices and the greatest uncertainty in generator earnings, due to the generally lower availability of VRE resources during this period. Our analysis provides important insights to investors on decision making, hedging strategies and portfolio management, as well as to regulators on effective planning to ensure sustainable and secure supply of electricity.

Title: Reciprocal tariffs will increase global emission: Evidence and numerical simulation results
Authors: Chunding LI, Meng LI, Jing LIU, Qiyuan XU
Abstract: The rise of protectionism and the growing fragmentation of global trade raise important yet under-explored questions about their environmental consequences. This paper investigates the CO2[jls-end-space/]emission consequences of reciprocal tariff wars with statistical regressions and structural quantitative simulations. Empirical analysis of the China-US tariff war in 2018 proved a significant increase in global CO 2 emissions. We develop a multi-country general equilibrium model that incorporates endogenous production reallocation and sectoral carbon intensities to quantify how tariff retaliation and trade fragmentation reshape global emission patterns. The results show that reciprocal tariffs systematically increase global CO2 emissions. Although tariffs reduce aggregate output, the structural reallocation of production toward more carbon-intensive regions, and the loss of economies of scale that increases emission intensity, dominates the contractionary effect, resulting in a net rise in world emissions. Trade conflicts involving systemically important economies, particularly China-US and US-EU, generate substantially larger emission increases than disputes with smaller trading partners. Moreover, trade decoupling produces significantly stronger emission increases than reciprocal tariff escalation, highlighting the climate risks associated with supply-chain fragmentation. These results underscore the importance of coordinating trade and climate policies to prevent trade fragmentation from undermining global decarbonization efforts.

Title: Higher-order moment connectedness between green cryptocurrencies and energy markets: The role of climate policy uncertainty
Authors: HaiFeng Wang, Qin Long, Xi Deng, Bangzhu Zhu, DengDeng Xiao
Abstract: We investigate the higher-order moment connectedness between green cryptocurrencies and energy markets using R2 decomposed connectedness approach. Moreover, we combine a time-varying Granger causality and a Markov regime-switching model to explore the effects of climate policy uncertainty (CPU) on the higher-order moment connectedness between green cryptos and energy markets. Our empirical findings show that: First, the spillover effects of skewness are the most pronounced, followed by kurtosis and volatility, indicating that higher-order moments detect market crisis risks more effectively. Green cryptocurrencies are major contributors in the higher-order moment spillover network. Second, the connectedness of higher-order moments is highly event-dependent, peaking during the COVID-19 pandemic and Russia-Ukraine conflict. Importantly, higher-order moment connectedness exhibits a relatively stronger response to the system between green cryptocurrencies and energy markets. Finally, climate policy uncertainty significantly affects pairwise spillovers, which is more sensitive to higher-order moments. Our study offers valuable information implications for regulators and investors.

Title: Are all COPs busted? The role of climate policy events for carbon pricing in compliance and voluntary markets
Authors: Patrick Behr, Riccardo Cosenza, Eric Nowak, Papa Orgen
Abstract: We study how four major climate policy events—COP 21 in Paris (2015), the Paris Agreement (2016), COP 26 in Glasgow (2021), and COP 28 in Dubai—affect carbon pricing in compliance and voluntary carbon markets. Using event study methodology, we show that carbon market participants significantly price COP outcomes. Co-integration tests further demonstrate that pricing relationships between compliance and voluntary carbon markets are stable when markets perceive policy outcomes as ambitious and credible, but weaken otherwise. Our results suggest that COPs function as policy-signalling events for carbon markets, with price responses reflecting market assessments of ambition, credibility, and implementation risk.

Title: Navigating uncertainty: Interconnections among carbon futures, geopolitical risk, and US energy markets
Authors: Ameet Kumar Banerjee, Ahmet Sensoy, Molla Ramizur Rahman
Abstract: This paper examines the impact of carbon futures and geopolitical conditions on the derivative segment of the energy market. We sourced data from January 4, 2017, to March 31, 2024, and bifurcated it into subperiods, with the second period coinciding with the Russia-Ukraine crisis, to analyze connectedness, risk embeddedness, and tolerances. We used time-varying parameter vector auto-regression (TVP-VAR) and a double-layer network framework to unveil the structural transformation of energy markets under geopolitical constraints. The study indicates that geopolitical risk is a significant contributor to spillover in both periods, with spillover being more pronounced in the second moment than in the first, particularly during the escalation of the war. Second, the double-layer network reveals that future market factors geopolitical distress resulting uncertainty. The tolerance for energy futures under geopolitical constraints declined during the Russia-Ukraine war, underscoring the vulnerability of energy assets during periods of war. These findings have significant implications for policymakers, investors, and risk managers. The results indicate that growing intensification can disrupt the functioning of energy markets and increase the risk of embeddedness in the interwoven markets.

Title: Severe weather and financial (in)stability
Authors: Claudia Foroni, Paolo Gelain, Marco Lorusso, Massimiliano Marcellino
Abstract: We quantify the effect of severe weather shocks on the US economy in an environment in which the economy can switch between periods of financial stability and financial instability, like the Great Recession. We estimate a New Keynesian dynamic stochastic general equilibrium model with banks and severe weather events. We show that severe weather shocks: (1) have a negative impact on real and financial US variables, sizeable only in periods of financial instability, but muted effects on nominal variables; (2) are never a relevant source of business cycle fluctuations; (3) transmit mainly via a deterioration in the quality of capital.

Title: European electricity prices in times of multiple crises
Authors: Mathias Mier
Abstract: The European electricity price crisis in 2022 can be attributed to three main factors: an increase in fuel prices, especially for natural gas and coal; a reduction in the availability of nuclear power plants in France; and a decline in hydroelectric power generation across the continent. This paper aims to elucidate the impact of these elements on electricity prices, taking into account the long-term implications of the EU ETS and the resulting CO2 prices. The European electricity price rises from 80 to 272 €/MWh in 2022. Most of this increase is due to higher fuel prices (84.6%), while French nuclear challenges contribute 9.4% and reduced European hydro generation 6.0%. French electricity prices even rise from 68 to 285 €/MWh, with nuclear problems contributing 22.8% to this price increase. The German price increase from 92 to 268 €/MWh is 82.4% due to higher fuel prices.

Title: The effects and financial impacts of wildfire smoke on solar photovoltaic power production in Alberta, Canada
Authors: Samantha M. Treacy, Alexandra B. Moura
Abstract: As reliance on solar photovoltaic (PV) generation grows, particularly in Alberta, accounting for the impact of wildfire smoke on solar energy production is crucial. This is particularly relevant in regions with high PV generation potential, such as Alberta, as they are often more vulnerable to frequent and intense wildfires. This study quantifies PV energy losses and financial impacts due to wildfire smoke in Alberta, using fine particulate matter 2.5 (PM2.5) as a proxy for smoke pollution. Historical weather and PM2.5 data, along with simulated PV production from actual completed, proposed, and under-construction projects, are used to train and test the model. The simulated data is validated against real production data. The six-year study (2018–2023) covers major wildfire years and employs machine learning techniques, particularly random forest regression, to isolate the effects of PM2.5 on solar production. Financial losses are estimated in Canadian dollars, adjusted for inflation to December 2023.Results show a PV production decline of up to 6.3% at a single solar site over six years, with an overall average reduction of 3.91% under severe conditions. The cumulative impact led to a 0.19% average generation loss, equating to over $4.5 million in financial losses. Higher smoke levels consistently correlate with greater solar energy losses, aligning with findings from other regions. The results of this study enhance our understanding of climate change impacts on solar energy, highlighting wildfire smoke as a relevant factor. As PV adoption expands, these findings offer valuable insights for decision-makers and operational planners, emphasizing the need for strategies to mitigate smoke-related disruptions and ensure energy reliability.

Title: Public preferences for energy sources in Italy
Authors: Peio Alcorta, Petr Mariel, Jürgen Meyerhoff, Giovanni Signorello, Maria De Salvo
Abstract: National Energy and Climate Plans (NECPs) are the primary roadmaps for European Union countries to achieve their 2030 targets for energy and climate, guiding investment decisions and a significant economic transformation. We conduct a discrete choice experiment to analyze preferences for different energy sources in Italy. We examine preferences regarding various attributes: the capacity shares of the most significant current and projected energy sources, the reliability of the supply of electricity, and cost. We use a latent class model to estimate the willingness to pay (WTP) for each attribute, finding that these preferences can be categorized into four groups. On average, we find overall support for the major renewable energy sources, opposition to fossil fuels and service interruptions, and strong opposition to nuclear power. Based on these results, we calculate the consumer surplus associated with the implementation of the national plan. The results show that the WTP aggregated over Italian households is lower than the investment levels estimated in the NECP. Spreading out the investments envisaged in the NECP over time can bring costs and benefits into better balance.

Title: Environmental tax shocks and economic growth: Global evidence from local projections
Authors: João Tovar Jalles, Alexandra Campmas
Abstract: This paper examines the macroeconomic effects of environmental tax shocks on economic growth using a panel of 76 advanced and developing economies over 1995–2021. We combine local projections with a novel identification strategy based on large, discretionary deviations in cyclically adjusted environmental tax revenues to isolate plausibly exogenous policy shocks. The validity of this approach is supported by Granger non-causality tests, predictability regressions, and pre-trend analyses. The results reveal heterogeneous and state-dependent effects. On average, environmental tax shocks generate modest but positive medium-term growth effects, becoming statistically significant after several years. These effects are stronger in emerging markets and developing economies (EMDEs), where revenues help relax fiscal constraints and support structural transformation, while remaining muted in advanced economies. Disaggregated results indicate that pollution and resource taxes drive the positive effects, whereas energy and transportation taxes have limited impact. Overall, the findings highlight the importance of context-sensitive policy design in aligning environmental taxation with growth objectives.

Title: Testing climate NGFS scenarios through the lens of a large-scale ABM for the Italian economy
Authors: Michele Catalano, Jacopo Di Domenico, Luca Riccetti
Abstract: We apply a data-driven, macroeconomic agent-based model calibrated on the Italian economy to study the green transition-specifically, the shift in electricity production from fossil fuels ("brown" sources) to renewable ("green") technologies-and the process of electrification, defined as the replacement of fossil fuel use with electricity. To better capture the dynamics of the energy sector, we extend the original macroeconomic model by expanding the energy sector into three subsectors, based on the Exiobase database, distinguishing between brown electricity, green electricity, and non-electricity energy sectors. We incorporate detailed information, particularly regarding carbon pricing and electrification, from three NGFS scenarios: Current Policies, Delayed Transition, and Net Zero. Based on these scenarios, we conduct a series of economic policy analyses. We find that a higher carbon tax leads to significant reductions in emissions while imposing only modest short-term economic costs on certain sectors, particularly those reliant on fossil fuels, along with a moderate increase in inflation. However, the green transition is associated with stronger long-run economic growth, primarily driven by increased investment in the renewable energy sector. Notably, when the carbon tax is combined with higher government consumption, the negative short-term effects on GDP are fully offset. Moreover, if the carbon tax is accompanied by green investment incentives, the resulting cost-push inflationary pressures can be partially mitigated. These findings highlight the potential of well-designed policy mixes to reconcile environmental objectives with sustained economic growth.

Title: Energy use rights trading policy, energy structure optimization and energy low-carbonization transformation: Evidence from China
Authors: Xuanxuan Jin, Xin Huang, Zhengxin Wang
Abstract: Under the “carbon peaking and carbon neutrality” targets of China, expediting the transition towards low-carbon energy stands as both the primary means to achieve synchronized economic stability and environmental amelioration, fostering the resolution of the increasingly acute supply-demand conflicts in the energy sector. This paper conducts an analysis, leveraging panel data from 2006 to 2022 across 30 Chinese provinces, focusing on the policy effects and mechanisms of the Energy Use Rights Trading Policy (ERTP) concerning the transition towards low-carbon energy. The study unveils the following insights: (1) ERTP, oriented by market mechanisms, accelerates the transition towards low-carbon energy, significantly elevating the low-carbon energy levels within the pilot policy regions. (2) The ERTP accelerates the low-carbon energy transition by promoting the optimization of the energy consumption structure. It significantly reduces the relative share of coal consumption while increasing the shares of petroleum and other energy sources. (3) ERTP demonstrates a policy exemplification effect, not only augmenting local low-carbon energy levels but also propelling adjacent regions towards low-carbon energy transitions. (4) The regional heterogeneity analysis indicates that the incentive effect of the ERTP on the low-carbon energy transition is mainly concentrated in the eastern regions and in areas where green and low-carbon technologies are not yet mature. This paper enriches the study of the driving mechanisms behind China's transition towards low-carbon energy policies and offers insights into enhancing the energy use rights trading system and fortifying the governance effectiveness of low-carbon policies.

Title: The impact of industrial opt-out from utility sponsored energy efficiency programs
Authors: Yu Ma, Gale Boyd, Matthew Doolin, Jennifer Weiss
Abstract: In the United States (US), industry accounts for approximately one-third of energy consumption. Rate of return demand-side management and energy efficiency programs are potential tools for regulated utilities to reduce energy use. However, many large customers are allowed to self-direct or opt-out of these programs, and there is typically no requirement to validate their energy savings. This study examines industrial energy efficiency among program participants and non-participants in the Carolinas by utilizing non-public Census of Manufacturing data along with data indicating firms' opt-out decisions. We compare the relative energy efficiency of plants that automatically stay in the programs versus those that choose to opt out. We first conduct a t-test to compare the average energy efficiency of two groups, and results suggest that opt-out plants are less efficient. However, the opt-out decisions may not be random. Large plants or plants belonging to large firms are more likely to opt out, possibly because they have greater access to information and resources. Therefore, we conduct a propensity score matching method to account for factors influencing the opt-out decision and enable a fair comparison between the groups. Results indicate that opt-out plants perform at least as well, or slightly better, than the stay-in plants. Our findings suggest that opt-out plants may not require utility program resources to achieve energy efficiency levels that are comparable to those of the stay-in group, at least for the sample we examined in this study.

Title: Beyond money: Homeowners’ preferences for the timing and application support of energy retrofit incentives
Authors: Shutong He, Queena K. Qian
Abstract: Improving the energy efficiency of residential buildings is essential for achieving long-term climate and energy goals, yet the uptake of home energy retrofits remains limited. While financial incentives are widely used to address upfront cost barriers, less is known about how incentive delivery mechanisms and associated transaction costs affect household investment decisions and welfare. This study conducts a discrete choice experiment with 796 Dutch homeowners to examine preferences for retrofit incentive schemes that vary in incentive timing (upfront discounts versus post-installation subsidies) and application support (energy coaches, contractors, and pre-filled forms). Estimating mixed logit models in both preference and willingness-to-pay space, we find that homeowners systematically prefer post-installation subsidies over upfront discounts, with a particularly strong aversion to discounts when handled by contractors. Application support, particularly personalised assistance, is highly valued and generates substantial welfare gains. Heterogeneity analysis shows that energy-vulnerable households (defined by lower income, lower investment literacy, and lower energy literacy) exhibit persistently low willingness to pay for future energy savings, and that the valuation of application support varies across vulnerability dimensions. Overall, the results demonstrate that reducing transaction costs through administrative support can partially substitute for higher financial incentives, with important implications for the cost-effectiveness and equity of energy retrofit policies.

Title: Does income moderate the carbon abatement impact of renewable energy? A global analysis of pooled and source-specific renewables, 1996–2023
Authors: Muhammad Fahad Khan Israr, Aurora A.C. Teixeira, Isabel Soares
Abstract: This study examines how income levels moderate the relationship between renewable energy and CO₂ emissions, focusing on heterogeneous environmental effects across stages of economic development. Using a panel of 168 countries over the period 1996–2023, the analysis incorporates interaction effects between income per capita and both aggregated and disaggregated renewable energy sources (hydropower, solar, wind, and biomass). The empirical strategy combines fixed-effects models with Driscoll–Kraay standard errors, bias-corrected estimators, quantile regression techniques, and system GMM estimators to address heteroscedasticity, cross-sectional dependence, and potential endogeneity. The results indicate that the relationship between renewable energy and CO₂ emissions varies systematically with income levels. At low income levels, renewable energy is associated with weak, statistically insignificant, or positive emission effects, consistent with transitional inefficiencies and a “green lag” phase. In contrast, higher income levels are associated with a stronger emission-reducing relationship between renewable energy and CO₂ emissions, consistent with a “green leap” pattern in more advanced economies. This nonlinear relationship is robust across alternative specifications, time periods, estimators, and functional forms, and holds for both aggregated and disaggregated renewable energy sources, with particularly strong effects for wind and solar energy in higher-income contexts. Estimated income thresholds suggest a gradual transition between regimes rather than a sharp structural break, reflecting continuous improvements in absorptive capacity, infrastructure, and system integration capabilities. Overall, the findings highlight that the environmental effectiveness of renewable energy is systematically conditioned by income-related capabilities, providing global evidence on heterogeneous diffusion dynamics and stage-dependent renewable energy effectiveness.

Title: Climate sensitivity of the Energy Security Index in China's prefecture-level cities: Identification and validation of nonlinear impacts from temperature and rainfall
Authors: Chien-Chiang Lee, Jinyang Zou
Abstract: Driven by China's “Dual Carbon” goals and rapid urbanization, climatic factors have become critical uncertainties for energy system stability. Using panel data from 282 Chinese cities (2005–2022) and a Double Machine Learning (DML) model, this paper analyzes the nonlinear impacts of temperature and rainfall on energy security (ES). We further employ impulse response analyses to examine dynamic climatic shocks and use the DML model to investigate the influence of extreme weather. Results show that low temperature and minimal rainfall significantly suppress ES, while moderate conditions exert boosting effects. Since 2015, the expansion of clean energy has intensified the negative shocks of low temperature. Heterogeneity analyses reveal that inland and less-developed cities' ES are more vulnerable; however, rich clean energy endowments and robust natural gas infrastructure mitigate these risks. Impulse response functions indicate that temperature shocks are more persistent than rainfall shocks. Additionally, extreme climate imposes significant inhibitory effects on ES. These findings provide a systematic framework for understanding climate-driven energy risks and offer evidence for building climate-resilient energy governance systems.

Title: Lighting up the future: The long-term effects of preschool exposure to electrification on female employment in rural China
Authors: Weihua Yu, Zengyang Yu, Xin Yao
Abstract: The Rural Hydropower Primary Electrification (RHPE) program, implemented during the 1980s and 1990s, marked an important transition from traditional energy sources to electricity in rural China. This paper employs a cohort difference-in-differences (DID) strategy to examine the long-term effects of the RHPE program on women's labor market outcomes. We find that preschool exposure to the RHPE program significantly improved girls' later-life labor market performance, whereas no comparable effect is observed for boys. We find little evidence that this effect operated through a reduction in household labor burdens. Instead, gender-differentiated improvements in human capital accumulation appear to be the main mechanism. Our findings highlight the gender-specific and long-lasting effects of rural electrification on individual economic outcomes.

Title: How customer geographic dispersion drives green innovation? Evidence from Chinese listed firms
Authors: Qian Liu, Han Liu, Libin Qin
Abstract: Against the backdrop of expanding corporate sales scope, we develop a novel indicator to capture customer geographic dispersion, and investigate whether and how a geographically dispersed customer base influences firms' green innovation. We find that greater customer geographic dispersion significantly promotes firms' green innovation, and the results are robust to a wide range of alternative variable constructions and identification strategies to mitigate endogeneity concerns. Mechanism analyses reveal two broad channels: pressure and capability. The pressure channel operates through stronger green pressure from customer regions and external governance from broad stakeholders, and capability channel operates through enhanced financing capacity that supports green innovation. The positive effect is more pronounced when firms have green background executives, when firms operate in heavily polluting industries and regions with more green finance resources. Our further analyses show that customer geographic dispersion promotes complementary green strategies, and its green-innovation effect is stronger when customers span multiple provinces. An economic consequence test confirms that the increase in green innovation spurred by customer geographic dispersion leads to a better environmental performance. Although it does not enhance corporate profit margins, as anticipated, such green innovation helps companies expand their market share and boost income. This study sheds light on the unexpected role of a novel customer geographic characteristic in firm green innovation along the supply chain.

Title: Persistent and transient inefficiency in China’s provincial energy demand: A four-component stochastic frontier model
Authors: Jessica Wai Yin Leung, Puguang Nie, Russell Smyth, Lin Zhang, Quanda Zhang, Xibin Zhang
Abstract: Improving energy efficiency is essential for advancing the clean energy transition and achieving decarbonization targets under the Paris Agreement, which makes accurate measurement of energy efficiency vitally important. Standard measures, such as energy intensity and two-step frontier procedures, can confound noise with inefficiency and induce omitted-variable bias. We develop a single-step four-component stochastic demand frontier that separates unobserved heterogeneity from inefficiency, decomposes inefficiency into persistent and transient components, and embeds observed drivers in the log-mean of the transient term. A Bayesian estimator delivers joint inference for the frontier, the decomposition, and driver effects. Applying the method to a panel of 30 provinces in China over 2003–2021, we find that omitting drivers tends to overstate energy efficiency, while including them reduces the share attributed to persistence to below one-half in several provinces and highlights the importance of short-run factors. Average transient efficiency is about 0.89, compared with roughly 0.69 for persistent efficiency. Overall, the unified design provides internally consistent, noise-robust efficiency measures and policy-relevant benchmarks that distinguish near-term operational levers from longer-horizon structural reforms.

Title: Carbon footprint of bank loans and bank lending: Global evidence using Bayesian approach
Authors: Duy Khanh Le
Abstract: This study provides the first global assessment of how the carbon footprint of bank loans (CFBL) influences bank lending behavior. We examine whether transition risks affect loan growth, non-performing loans, and bank spreads, with a specific focus on the differential impacts of direct (Scope 1) versus indirect (Scope 2 & 3) emissions. Using panel data from 36 countries (2005–2018), we employ a Bayesian regression framework to capture the inherent uncertainties of climate risks, complemented by two-step System GMM to address endogeneity. The findings reveal that while banks have integrated direct transition risks into their lending strategies, they significantly overlook the “hidden” carbon footprints within supply chains. This oversight leads to an accumulation of systemic risk that current bank spreads fail to adequately offset. Our research contributes a novel methodological approach and provides critical evidence for policymakers to mandate transparency regarding indirect carbon exposures in the global financial system.

Title: The impact of energy price shocks on US local industries: A state-level analysis
Authors: Minsu Kim, Stephan J. Goetz
Abstract: Economic activity consumes large amounts of energy, making modern economies especially vulnerable to energy price shocks. Following such a shock, firms can adjust by reducing output or energy used per unit of output. Here we use annual panel data for the 50 US States to examine how local industries have adapted to energy price changes from 2001 to 2019. We estimate a recursive dynamic system to model how energy prices affect output both directly and indirectly through induced capital adjustment and energy intensity. We find that energy price increases reduce local GDP in the short run but also lead to long-term increases in energy efficiency. Output contracts in the short run, but dynamic efficiency gains mitigate these losses: on average, reduced energy intensity offsets between 2% to 5% of the short run decline in GDP. We interpret these dynamics as evidence of induced efficiency adaptation via capital accumulation at the state level, which decouples energy consumption from economic growth as energy prices rise.

Title: Carbon emissions and financial flexibility: International evidence
Authors: Chien-Chiang Lee, Chih-Wei Wang, Tsai-Yun Hu, Weizheng Lin, Ai Ngoc Nhan Le
Abstract: This paper examines the relationship between firms' carbon performance and financial flexibility using a comprehensive sample of international firms from 2007 to 2024. We find that companies with stronger carbon performance are better able to preserve spare debt capacity, thereby enhancing their financial flexibility. To mitigate concerns of endogeneity and establish causal inference, we adopt multiple identification strategies. Our mechanism analysis highlights two key channels: growth opportunities and working capital efficiency. While both contribute to the carbon–flexibility link, improvements in working capital management emerge as the dominant pathway. These findings suggest that effective carbon management not only strengthens firms' environmental responsibility but also plays a critical role in improving financial resilience, with broader implications for sustainable corporate strategies and capital market assessments.

Title: Carbon leakage and carbon tax differentiation: Evidence from a developing economy
Authors: Duy Chinh Nguyen, Nhat Duy Lai
Abstract: Carbon leakage is conventionally attributed to import substitution. This paper provides evidence that in assembly-oriented economies with dense global value chain (GVC) integration, imported intermediates complement domestic output, generating a demand-destruction channel: carbon taxation contracts domestic production and simultaneously reduces demand for imported inputs. Using a computable general equilibrium (CGE) model of Vietnam, we quantify sector-specific leakage rates and evaluate four carbon tax designs. The aggregate unilateral import-substitution leakage rate is 0.475 at ten dollars per tonne of CO 2 in the single-country framework, interpretable as an upper bound on international leakage from the import-substitution channel; the corresponding multi-region GTAP-E benchmark, which captures residual global emission reallocation after foreign supply, world-price, and bilateral-diversion responses, returns 0.061. Textiles, metals, and machinery exhibit negative leakage in the single-country framework because contracted production proportionally reduces demand for imported intermediates; the multi-region GTAP-E model reproduces this pattern for textiles, machinery, and iron-and-steel. A leakage-weighted differentiated carbon tax delivers 24% less net abatement than a uniform tax under a revenue-neutral schedule, showing that a partial-equilibrium leakage-weighting heuristic performs poorly under general-equilibrium input-output spillovers. Combining the carbon tax with an EU-style carbon border adjustment reduces single-country leakage, while the multi-region benchmark shows near-zero effect on aggregate leakage. Revenue recycling to the poorest rural households reverses regressive welfare incidence and raises net abatement through a demand-injection mechanism linked to non-homothetic consumption. These results inform Vietnam's emerging carbon market and, subject to analogous GVC-assembly integration, carbon pricing design in other lower-middle-income economies.

Title: Asymmetric fuel demand in the UK industrial sectors
Authors: Akinsehinwa Sharimakin, Morakinyo O. Adetutu
Abstract: This study investigates asymmetric demand responses in UK industrial gas and electricity consumption using the Dargay and Gately (1995) decomposition framework. We employ random-effects hierarchical models to account for sectoral heterogeneity and obtain robust long-run elasticity estimates. The results indicate that most specifications favour asymmetric demand responses, with electricity demand exhibiting greater sensitivity to changes in energy price exposure and economic activity than gas demand. Evidence on the role of technical progress is mixed and appears to be model-dependent. Most estimated long-run elasticities are inelastic, suggesting that policies relying primarily on energy price signals or changes in economic activity may have limited effectiveness in achieving energy and environmental objectives. The comparatively strong responsiveness of electricity demand implies that industrial electrification in the UK may proceed more slowly than anticipated, as increases in aggregate energy prices, mediated through sectoral exposure, could encourage firms to substitute toward relatively less costly fuels. Sectoral differences further underscore the importance of accounting for variations in production technologies and structural characteristics rather than imposing homogeneous behavioural responses across industries. Overall, the findings have important implications for UK industrial energy policy and highlight firms' capacity to adjust their energy consumption patterns in response to evolving economic conditions.

Title: Editorial Board
Commonality in systemic risk from green and conventional energy
Authors: Md Akhtaruzzaman, Molla Ramizur Rahman
Abstract: Our study is a novel attempt to examine the sub-industry sectors of conventional energy (i.e., oil & gas, crude production, oil refinery & marketing, and oil equipment and services) and the sub-industry sector of green energy (i.e., renewable energy) to analyse the systemic risk and commonality. The results show that the systemic risk for green energy has decreased since 2006, indicating a shift towards net-zero emissions. Further, we develop a systemic contagion index (SCI) for green and conventional energy. The SCI shows that green energy has lower contagion than conventional energy. However, conventional energy appears to create lower contagion during crises, indicating its herding characteristics and investors' preference for conventional energy during crises. A mild systemic risk commonality between green and conventional energy provides an opportunity to shift towards green energy, thus enhancing the possibility of achieving net-zero emissions. These findings provide guidance to policymakers to build the global green and conventional energy policy to achieve net-zero emissions in 2050.

Title: Institutional investor behaviour and the energy transition: A complexity framework for sustainable finance in the UK
Authors: Kandace Persad, Bing Xu, Philip Greening
Abstract: Despite sustainable investment flows having increased significantly over the past decade for transforming the current energy system, a large investment gap remains. This research explores the complex links between institutional investors' expectations on the speed of the energy transition and their sustainability-related investment behaviours. Through in-depth semi-structured interviews with institutional investors, we construct a complex system model using a causal mapping approach, illustrating complex relationships within the sustainable investment system. Our contribution involves the development of multi-layer cognitive maps for different types of institutional investors, followed by a composite causal map that dissects key investment behaviours and investor expectations. Results reveal interlinked concepts influencing investment behaviour and highlight feedback loops with potential amplifying effects on investor expectations and investment behaviour. Two critical feedback loops emerge: 1) the interplay between political and financial support for the energy transition and the associated cost, and 2) the intricate relationship between sustainability factors and asset valuation. Addressing these interconnected issues simultaneously and monitor negative feedback loops that may curtail sustainable finance flows are vital. The results reveal heterogeneities amongst institutional investors such as fiduciary duties, stranded assets, the importance of fossil fuels in the energy system. In sum, our insights provide a foundation for holistic energy policies and a reference system for evaluating policies aimed at accelerating green finance.

Title: Climate change, environmental policies in the housing sector of Italy, and the impact on social welfare
Authors: Alberto Massacci, Shajara Ul-Durar, Noman Arshed, Arshian Sharif
Abstract: The European Commission has significantly increased its focus on sustainability issues and the growing energy deficit. Residential consumption has been identified as one of the most energy-intensive segments, prompting the Commission to propose an Energy Performance of Buildings Directive. This directive aims to establish minimum standards for buildings to be met within specified timeframes. In this context, it is crucial to identify and address all potential drawbacks of such measures, ensuring that not only environmental but also social and economic aspects of sustainability are considered. This paper examines the impact of a fiscal incentive, called the Superbonus, implemented by the Italian government to promote sustainable investments and facilitate the recovery of the real estate sector following the pandemic. The work contributes to the growing literature on climate policies by focusing on the indirect effects on households and welfare through the analysis of the allocation of government resources across geographical areas and its impact on the housing market. The study employs a difference-in-differences approach with a continuous treatment variable to analyze the impact of the Superbonus on the real estate market, using data from Milan's residential market over the period 2016–2021. The results indicate that, while the fiscal incentive may have produced undesired welfare effects, the impact on the housing market led to a more equitable redistribution, albeit limited to those who already owned properties. The paper disentangles the main underlying mechanisms behind these effects, contributing both from an academic perspective and offering several political insights.

Title: The effect of pricing instruments on CO2 emissions: Empirical evidence from Australia
Authors: Daniel Kraynak, Govinda Timilsina, Anna Alberini
Abstract: This paper investigates the emission reduction effects of a mix of market-based climate policies in Australia, where a dramatic ramp-up of incentives for renewable electricity generation since 2009 was paired with a carbon tax that was introduced in 2012 and repealed in 2014. A synthetic control method is employed to estimate the joint effect of these policies, finding that the renewable energy incentives and carbon tax policies together reduced Australia’s annual per capita CO2 emissions by 7.15% on average between 2009 and 2018. The emission reduction impacts were attenuated but not reversed when the carbon price was repealed in 2014 and the renewable targets were softened in 2015. We also find that the policy mix did not reduce the production of Australian coal and may in fact have expanded its export. The findings suggest that even short-lived climate change mitigation policies can have substantial and persistent effects on emissions.

Title: Climate change economics in Vietnam: Redefining economic impact
Authors: Christian Otto, Christoph Schult, Thomas Vogt
Abstract: Vietnam, a low middle-income economy, grapples with considerable climate impacts, primarily driven by heat waves, sea level rise, and tropical cyclones. Under ongoing global warming, these extreme weather events are projected to further intensify. We use a dynamic general equilibrium model to study economic transition dynamics from 2015 to 2100, accounting for heat-induced labor productivity losses, agricultural land loss from sea level rise, and residential property damage from tropical cyclones. We compare a Paris-compatible strong mitigation scenario where global warming is limited to well below 2 °C above preindustrial levels to a strong emission scenario where warming reaches 4–5 °C. We find that the impacts of climate change on output and investment are highly uncertain, with differences between the two emission scenarios remaining statistically insignificant until the end of the century, despite substantially higher climate forcing in the latter. By contrast, consumption losses are significantly larger under the high emission scenario. These negative impacts are primarily driven by heat-induced labor productivity losses, while TCs are the main source of uncertainty. Our findings highlight the need for analytical frameworks to capture the different channels through which climate and climate change affect economic development, rather than focusing mainly on output-related damage, as done in many existing studies.

Title: Energy markets reforms and renewable energy in Africa: Do public–private partnership matter?
Authors: Kwamivi Mawuli Gomado, Amandine Laré
Abstract: Access to reliable, affordable, and sustainable energy is crucial for economic growth, industrialization, and social development. However, a significant portion of the Sub-Saharan population still lacks electricity, hindering both economic and social progress. This article examines the impact of electricity market reforms on the production and consumption of renewable energy, with a particular emphasis on the role of public–private partnerships (PPPs). The analysis is based on a panel of 18 African countries from 1990 to 2014 and utilizes local projections in conjunction with an augmented inverse probability weighted regression adjustment (LP-AIPW) estimator to mitigate selection bias. The findings reveal that reforms generally enhance renewable energy production in the short and medium term, while their effect on consumption is more modest and primarily evident in the medium term. Periods characterized by PPP projects within the energy sector during the analyzed period experience greater and more sustained benefits, underscoring the importance of integrating market reforms with complementary policies. Overall, these results highlight the potential of market reforms and PPPs to expedite Africa’s energy transition and achieve universal access to clean, reliable, and affordable energy, in alignment with Sustainable Development Goal 7.

Title: Coupling a stock-flow consistent macroeconomic model with an energy system optimisation model to study the impacts of the energy transition in Colombia
Authors: Pierre Jacques, Stanislas Augier, Santiago Barbosa, Devrim Yilmaz, Hervé Jeanmart, Antoine Godin
Abstract: The green transition presents a major economic and financial risk to fossil fuel exporting countries. Colombia is a good example of this: the country will have to cope with significant economic and financial imbalances due to the loss of exports, at the same moment when it tries to mobilise resources to invest in the decarbonisation of its own energy system. To study the intertwine between the energy transition and macroeconomic trends, we present a novel coupling between a Stock-Flow Consistent (SFC) macroeconomic model and an Energy System Optimisation Model (ESOM). This coupled model is applied to Colombia to simulate a variety of scenarios. The results especially highlight the joint dynamics between the energy transition, cross-border financial flows and the national currency exchange rate. Overall, the results suggest that the Colombian domestic energy transition, after a ramp-up during its first decade, can have significant macroeconomic impacts, positive or negative depending on the chosen strategy. Based on this pioneering work, several avenues for future research are put forward, to refine the feedback loops in our model of the economy-finance-energy system.

Title: Beliefs, evidence, and climate action
Authors: Mark C. Freeman, Ben Groom, Frikk Nesje, Gernot Wagner
Abstract: We assess how changes in the scientific consensus around equilibrium climate sensitivity (ECS), as captured by the IPCC’s Fifth (AR5) and Sixth (AR6) Assessment Reports, impact policymakers’ willingness to take climate action. Taking the IPCC’s reports at face value, the ECS estimates in AR6 would have lowered a policymaker’s willingness to act on climate relative to AR5 due to a narrower “likely” range. However, Bayesian updating may reverse this conclusion. An accuracy-motivated policymaker who was not convinced to take greater climate action by the evidence in AR5 may be more likely to increase their investment in clean energy by the evidence in AR6.

Title: Can grid tariffs be fair and efficient? A comprehensive evaluation of tariff designs for smart electric vehicle integration
Authors: Nico Brinkel, Floris van Montfoort
Abstract: The rapid adoption of electric vehicles (EVs) is increasing electricity demand and raising capacity requirements on distribution grids that in many countries are already near their limits. Grid tariffs that reflect capacity costs can promote more efficient use of the grid infrastructure and encourage smart charging of EVs, including optimization of the timing and speed of charging to reduce peak loads. However, most existing tariffs provide limited incentives for such behavior. In recent years, various alternative tariff designs have been proposed, yet comprehensive evidence on their impacts remains limited. This study introduces a framework to evaluate tariff structures against regulatory principles, including efficiency, fairness, and simplicity.
